## **EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**

The Western Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Council (WPRFMC) is the policy-making organization for the management of fisheries in the Exclusive Economic Zone or EEZ (3-200 nmi from shore) in the Western Pacific Region.

--- SENTENCE 49 ---
This includes the waters surrounding the U.S. Pacific Islands: State of Hawaii, Territories of American Samoa and Guam, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) and the unincorporated Other U.S. Pacific Islands.

--- SENTENCE 50 ---
WPRFMC currently has Fishery Management Plans (FMPs) in place for fisheries of four species groups: crustaceans, precious corals, bottomfish and seamount groundfish, and pelagics.

--- SENTENCE 51 ---
WPRFMC is now interested in determining if there are any current management needs for coral reef resources in the region.

--- SENTENCE 52 ---
In order to do this, the Council requires a detailed summary of the extent and condition of the coral reef resources, their patterns of use, and the existing management regimes.

--- SENTENCE 53 ---
WPRFMC is also interested in the status of special management issues which may be affecting coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 54 ---
This includes the presence of specialized coral reef fisheries (the live reef fish and aquarium fish trades) and the extent of habitat degradation caused by human impacts (including over fishing, sedimentation, nutrient loading, coastal construction, pollution and contamination, destructive fishing practices, tourism, recreation and military activities).

--- SENTENCE 55 ---
The objective of this report is to summarize this information.

--- SENTENCE 56 ---
The scope includes a synthesis of the information contained in scientific papers and unpublished reports, as well as comments from representatives of local government agencies and knowledgeable individuals (scientists, fishermen and dive operators).

--- SENTENCE 57 ---
This project has been completed in two stages.

--- SENTENCE 58 ---
First, Dr. Cindy Hunter was contracted to do a preliminary assessment of the issue.

--- SENTENCE 59 ---
Dr. Hunter produced a report that summarized coral reef area, jurisdiction, coral reef condition and the existing patterns of use in the region.

--- SENTENCE 60 ---
Second, Dr. Alison Green was contracted to prepare a more detailed assessment of the issue.

--- SENTENCE 61 ---
Three other consultants were also contracted to assist Dr. Green by summarizing the condition of the resources, and the most recent fisheries statistics for three of the five areas (Dr. Alan Freidlander in Hawaii, Robert Myers in Guam and John Gourley in CNMI).

--- SENTENCE 62 ---
The present report is a synthesis of the available information, which encompasses the results of the reports by the other contractors: Hunter (1995), Friedlander (1996), Myers (1997) and Gourley (1997).

#### Present Status and Patterns of Use

The coral reef resources in the U.S. Pacific Islands cover an estimated area of 15,852 km<sup>2</sup>, most of which (10,762 km<sup>2</sup>) is located in the EEZ (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 63 ---
The vast majority of the coral reef area in the EEZ is located in Hawaii, with smaller areas present in the other parts of the region.

!

--- SENTENCE 64 ---
A. Coral reef area in nearshore waters and the Exclusive Economic Zone (0-3 nm and 3-shore respectively) in each location in the U.S. Pacific Islands (modified from

Coral reef condition and utilization patterns vary throughout the region (Tables A&B).

--- SENTENCE 65 ---
The majority of the reefs in the EEZ (88% by area) appear to be in good condition, largely because they are remote from major human population centers.

--- SENTENCE 66 ---
Similarly, these reefs appear to be unfished or only lightly used, because of their remoteness, and in some cases, their protected status.

--- SENTENCE 67 ---
Exceptions include the more accessible offshore banks in Hawaii, Guam and CNMI (Penguin, Galvez and Esmeralda respectively) and the banks surrounding the island of Farallon de Medinilla in CNMI, which are heavily fished.

--- SENTENCE 68 ---
However, much of the fishing in these areas is for bottomfish, with an unknown component of reef species included in the catch.

--- SENTENCE 69 ---
The relatively good condition of most reefs in federal waters is in stark contrast to many of the reefs in nearshore state or territorial waters, which appear to have been degraded by a combination of natural and anthropogenic effects, including habitat degradation and overfishing.

--- SENTENCE 70 ---
In general, nearshore reefs that are close to human population centers tend to be more heavily used and in worse condition than those in more remote areas (Tables A&B).

--- SENTENCE 71 ---

--- SENTENCE 84 ---
The coral reef fisheries of the U.S. Pacific Islands tend to be dominated by reef fishes (60-90% of catch), and the total 'nominal' reef fish production is estimated to be 1,000 tons (Dalzell et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 85 ---
Most of the catch comes from Hawaii (700 t), followed by American Samoa (176 t), CNMI (84 t) and Guam (39 t).

--- SENTENCE 86 ---
Minor catches have also been recorded in the Other U.S. Pacific Islands.

--- SENTENCE 87 ---
Invertebrates comprise most of the remainder of the catch (10-40%), although the taxa that are important vary among islands.

--- SENTENCE 88 ---
For example, molluscs, echinoderms, and crustaceans are locally important in American Samoa, CNMI, and Hawaii respectively.

--- SENTENCE 89 ---
Corals and live rock comprise only an incidental part of the catch (mostly precious corals), since stony coral and live rock collecting is illegal in states throughout the region.

--- SENTENCE 90 ---
Algal harvesting is also believed to be an important component of the fishery in some locations (especially Hawaii), but the size of the harvest is unknown.

--- SENTENCE 91 ---
The majority of the coral reef fisheries in the U.S. Pacific Islands occur in nearshore waters (80-100%), with only a small component (<20%) occurring in the EEZ.

--- SENTENCE 92 ---
The following is an overview of the results of the assessment for each location.

--- SENTENCE 93 ---
For the purposes of this report, coral reefs were defined as "substratum adjacent to coastlines (or

on shoals) from depths of 1-100 m that is primarily composed of hard-bottom" (Hunter 1995).

--- SENTENCE 94 ---
This definition led to problems of overlap between coral reef fisheries and other fisheries (see *Overlap with Existing FMPs* below).

--- SENTENCE 95 ---
The main problem was the overlap with the bottomfish fishery, which is generally considered to include two components that can be separated on the basis of depth and species complex: the shallow-water (< 150 m) emperor based bottomfish fishery and the deep-water (150-250 m) eteline snapper and grouper based bottomfish fishery.

--- SENTENCE 96 ---
Therefore, many of the species in the shallow-water bottomfish fishery could also be considered "reef species" as defined in this report.

--- SENTENCE 97 ---
Consequently, the shallow-water bottomfish fishery is also discussed in some locations (mostly CNMI).

--- SENTENCE 98 ---
## State of Hawaii

By far the largest coral reef area in federal waters is located in Hawaii (10,004 km²), of which most is situated in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands (NWHI: 9,124 km²).

--- SENTENCE 99 ---
Surveys of the NWHI show that they support healthy coral reefs with high standing stocks of many reef fishes.

--- SENTENCE 100 ---
These resources receive little impact because of their protected status, remoteness and harsh seasonal weather conditions.

--- SENTENCE 101 ---
However, some recreational fishing does occur by occasional visitors to the area, including federal government personnel and visitors to Midway Atoll.

--- SENTENCE 102 ---
Data are not yet available for this fishery, although it is assumed to be minor.

--- SENTENCE 103 ---
The Main Hawaiian Islands (MHI) also comprise a reasonably large area of coral reef in federal waters (880km²), almost all of which is located on Penguin Bank off Molokai.

--- SENTENCE 104 ---
Little is known about the condition of these reefs.

--- SENTENCE 105 ---
In contrast, many of the reefs in near shore waters in the MHI are known to have been badly degraded as a result of over fishing, urbanization and development.

--- SENTENCE 106 ---
Commercial fisheries catch statistics for Hawaii reveal that coral reef fisheries account for 10.2% of the weight (1,570,285 lb) and 10.5% of the value (\$3,392,645) of the total mean annual commercial catch.

--- SENTENCE 107 ---
Less than 12% of all inshore fishes were caught in federal waters (32,018 lb and \$65,402).

--- SENTENCE 108 ---
In contrast, approximately half (51% by weight) of the State's reported commercial landings of Kona crab were taken on Penguin Bank between 1990 and 1995 (14,191 lb and \$57,436).

--- SENTENCE 109 ---
However, the commercial crab landings on Penguin Bank are only a minor component of the total fisheries catch for the State (<1% by weight).

--- SENTENCE 110 ---
Recreational catch in Hawaii is unknown, although it is assumed to be equal to or greater than the commercial catch for some important target species.

--- SENTENCE 111 ---
Most of the recreational fishing for reef species occurs in state waters close to shore, although Penguin Bank is believed to support a substantial, but undocumented, recreational fishery for deepwater snappers and groupers.

--- SENTENCE 112 ---
This study was hindered by the absence of good quality fisheries statistics for the MHI.

--- SENTENCE 113 ---
Future studies should be encouraged that would provide a better assessment of the catch from both commercial and recreational fishermen in the MHI, especially on Penguin Bank.

--- SENTENCE 114 ---
A resource assessment of Penguin Bank and more reefs in the NWHI would also be of value.

--- SENTENCE 115 ---
## Territory of American Samoa

The coral reef resources of American Samoa are limited in area (total =296 km²), and only a small portion is located within federal waters (25 km²).

--- SENTENCE 116 ---
A recent resource assessment showed that the near shore reefs in territorial waters vary in condition throughout the archipelago.

--- SENTENCE 117 ---
Reefs on the main island of Tutuila are in the worst condition because of a combination of natural and anthropogenic effects (hurricanes, coral bleaching, pollution, sedimentation etc.), while the reefs on the more remote and less populated islands tend to be in good condition.

--- SENTENCE 118 ---
Virtually nothing is known of the condition of the reefs in federal waters, because they are relatively inaccessible.

--- SENTENCE 119 ---
However, it is assumed that they are in better condition than the near shore reefs, because they are in deeper water and remote from most human activities.

--- SENTENCE 120 ---
Recent fisheries statistics from American Samoa show that coral reef fisheries have accounted for 62% of the catch (339,730 lb) and 70% of the value (\$619,009) of the value of the total mean landings in the Territory over the last few years.

--- SENTENCE 121 ---
The actual total for coral reef fisheries is probably higher than this for two reasons.

--- SENTENCE 122 ---
First, this estimate does not include the shoreline artisanal catch, which is assumed to be substantial.

--- SENTENCE 123 ---
Second, the coral reef harvest will include an unknown proportion of the shallow-water bottomfish catch, because of overlap between the two fisheries (see above).

--- SENTENCE 124 ---
However, the mean annual harvest of the bottomfish fishery in American Samoa is small (23,754 lb with a local market value of \$45,722), and unlikely to contribute a substantial amount to this total.

--- SENTENCE 125 ---
Most of the landings in the known coral reef fisheries in American Samoa are reef fishes (215,897 lb), molluscs (73,112 lb) and echinoderms (43,384 lb), although small amounts of crustaceans (7,337 lb) are also harvested.

--- SENTENCE 126 ---
Recent fisheries statistics show that the shoreline coral reef fishery appears to be in decline, possibly because of habitat degradation.

--- SENTENCE 127 ---
All of the coral reef fisheries in American Samoa occur in near shore territorial waters.

--- SENTENCE 128 ---
However, since most of the bottomfishing occurs in federal waters, and some of the species in this fishery can be considered reef fishes, then it is possible that a small proportion of the coral reef fishery also occurs in federal waters.

--- SENTENCE 129 ---
However, this catch is assumed to be minor, since no major commercial fisheries operate in federal waters in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 130 ---
A resource assessment of these reefs and their patterns of use would be useful, but is not a high priority.

--- SENTENCE 131 ---
X

## Territory of Guam

The total coral reef area in federal waters in Guam is small relative to the other states and territories (110 km²).

--- SENTENCE 132 ---
However, these reefs account for approximately 60% of the coral reef area in Guam.

--- SENTENCE 133 ---
All of the reefs in the EEZ in Guam are offshore banks and shoals, which are relatively inaccessible.

--- SENTENCE 134 ---
As such, they are much less heavily fished than the nearshore resources, and only account for <20% of the 235-335,000 lb of coral reef resources harvested annually in the Territory in recent years.

--- SENTENCE 135 ---
Most of these harvested resources (>90%) were finfish.

--- SENTENCE 136 ---
Virtually no information exists on the condition of the coral reef resources in federal waters in Guam, and a resource assessment of these reefs would be useful.

--- SENTENCE 137 ---
On the basis of anecdotal information, it is appears that most of these reefs are in good condition because of their isolation.

--- SENTENCE 138 ---
The exception may be Galvez Bank, which has been reported to be over fished in recent years.

--- SENTENCE 139 ---
In contrast, many of the reefs in Guam's territorial waters appear to have been badly degraded by over fishing and other human impacts (especially sedimentation).

## Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI)

--- SENTENCE 140 ---
CNMI accounts for the second largest coral reef area in the U.S. Pacific Islands (area=579 km²).

--- SENTENCE 141 ---
At present, all coral reef resources in CNMI are under federal jurisdiction (0-200 nmi from shore), although the local government currently manages these resources.

--- SENTENCE 142 ---
The majority of the coral reef resources in CNMI (534 km²) are located 3-200 nmi from shore, most of which is accounted for by Farallon de Medinilla and submerged shoals, reefs and banks (311 km² and 204 km² respectively).

--- SENTENCE 143 ---
Limited information suggests that most of the near shore reefs in CNMI are in good condition, except in some locations on the southern islands, where there are major population centers and there has been extensive coastal development and over fishing (especially on Saipan).

--- SENTENCE 144 ---
Some of the near shore reefs may have also suffered as a result of recent military (e.g. on Farallon de Medinilla and Rota) and volcanic activities (e.g. on Pagan).

--- SENTENCE 145 ---
Virtually nothing is known of the condition of the banks and shoals in the EEZ in CNMI, although most are assumed to be in good condition because of their isolation.

--- SENTENCE 146 ---
Coral reef fisheries in CNMI appear to be mostly limited to near shore reefs, especially on the main islands of Saipan, Rota and Tinian.

--- SENTENCE 147 ---
Unfortunately, it is difficult to assess the total harvest of these fisheries, because of shortcomings in the local fisheries statistics.

--- SENTENCE 148 ---
These include limitations in geographic coverage (mostly limited to Saipan) and the poor quality of some of the data.

--- SENTENCE 149 ---
For example, some of the data cannot be subdivided into strata that will allow for a detailed analysis of the catch by area, depth, and in some cases, taxa.

--- SENTENCE 150 ---
In particular, coral reef fish are difficult to separate from bottomfish in some of the existing databases.

--- SENTENCE 151 ---
All of the recent statistics that are available for the coral reef fisheries in CNMI are for

the commercial fisheries.

--- SENTENCE 152 ---
Most of these fisheries take place in the nearshore waters on the southern islands of Saipan, Tinian, Aguijan and Rota.

--- SENTENCE 153 ---
Data from the commercial purchase survey show that at least 136,653–177,377 lb of coral reef fish and 2,240-3,425 lb of spiny lobster were landed each year from 1992-1994.

--- SENTENCE 154 ---
Commercial fisheries for trochus and sea cucumbers were also re-opened for the first time in recent history, and a total of 268,068 sea cucumbers (168,235 lb live weight) were harvested over an 18 month period from 1995 to 1996.

--- SENTENCE 155 ---
No harvest estimates are available for the trochus fishery.

--- SENTENCE 156 ---
Very little is known of the coral reef fisheries in the northern islands, although the catch is believed to minor in most years.

--- SENTENCE 157 ---
The exception was in 1995, when the near shore fringing reefs of six of the northern islands (especially Anatahan and Sarigan) were fished commercially for seven months of the year.

--- SENTENCE 158 ---
During that time, these islands yielded a harvest of 15, 335 kg of reef fish and 380 spiny lobsters.

--- SENTENCE 159 ---
An unknown proportion of the bottomfish landings in CNMI may also be classified as part of the coral reef fishery, based on species captured and depth fished (see above).

--- SENTENCE 160 ---
However, it is difficult to do so, because much of the catch is unidentified (29-51%), and the depth at which the fish were captured is unknown.

--- SENTENCE 161 ---
However, two of the commercial bottomfishing operations have recently started targeting shallow-water species (< 100 m deep) in the northern islands, and the proportion of "reef species" in the catch may have increased.

--- SENTENCE 162 ---
Furthermore, since much of this fishery takes place on the extensive bank at Farallon de Medinilla, it is possible that a moderate fishery for "reef species" is taking place in the EEZ of the CNMI, which is currently classified as part of the shallow-water bottomfish fishery.

--- SENTENCE 163 ---
Virtually no information is available on the inshore subsistence and recreational catch of coral reef species in CNMI at present, since the data from the Inshore and Offshore Creel Surveys have not been properly analyzed because of data quality problems.

--- SENTENCE 164 ---
However, this catch is assumed to be substantial, especially in the more heavily populated areas such as Saipan Lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 165 ---
Coral reef species harvested in this fishery include reef fishes and invertebrates, as well as small quantities of marine algae.

--- SENTENCE 166 ---
Anecdotal information suggests that most of the reefs in the EEZ receive very little fishing pressure, since local fishermen do not like to venture far from shore.

--- SENTENCE 167 ---
The exceptions are the banks that are relatively close to the main islands (e.g. Esmeralda) and the extensive bank at Farallon de Medinilla, which are heavily fished.

--- SENTENCE 168 ---
Better quality data is clearly needed before the management needs for the coral reef resources in CNMI can be adequately determined.

--- SENTENCE 169 ---
In particular, there is a strong need for a good resource assessment of the reefs in CNMI, which will describe the coral reef resources and their current condition.

--- SENTENCE 170 ---
There is also a need for a study on the patterns of utilization of coral reef resources in CNMI, especially relating to the shallow-water

bottomfish fishery at Farallon de Medinilla.

--- SENTENCE 171 ---
Fortunately, this seems to be underway at present.

## Other Unincorporated U.S. Pacific Islands

--- SENTENCE 172 ---
The total coral reef area on these remote islands and atolls is 620 km<sup>2</sup>, of which 112 km<sup>2</sup> are currently under WPRFMC jurisdiction.

--- SENTENCE 173 ---
Little is known about the status of most of these reefs, although the majority are assumed to be pristine because they are remote from human activities.

--- SENTENCE 174 ---
The exceptions are reefs that are immediately adjacent to islands occupied by the military, where coastal construction and pollution and contamination have affected coral reef health.

--- SENTENCE 175 ---
The majority of these islands and atolls are unfished, because of their remoteness and protected status as National Wildlife Refuges.

--- SENTENCE 176 ---
The main exceptions are Johnston and Wake, where fishing is a popular sport among the resident work forces.

--- SENTENCE 177 ---
However, it appears that these atolls are only lightly fished, and that all of the fishing takes place in near shore waters.

--- SENTENCE 178 ---
A detailed quantitative survey of these reefs would be useful to clearly identify the coral reef resources that are protected in these areas.

--- SENTENCE 179 ---
## **Management Needs**

This assessment did not reveal any major management issues for the coral reef resources in the EEZ of the Western Pacific Region at present, since most of the reefs are in good condition and only lightly used, if at all.

--- SENTENCE 180 ---
However, some issues may warrant Council consideration.

--- SENTENCE 181 ---
One issue is the use of the island of Farallon de Medinilla (FDM) as a military bombing target in CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 182 ---
This island is of particular interest to the Council, since it accounts for the largest area of coral reef in the EEZ outside of the State of Hawaii.

--- SENTENCE 183 ---
At present, local fishermen are harvesting shallow-water bottomfish at FDM, and they believe that the bombing is impacting the fisheries resources in the area.

--- SENTENCE 184 ---
The ongoing use of the island as a target is now being re-assessed, with the intent of continuing or expanding training operations.

--- SENTENCE 185 ---
A comprehensive assessment of the fisheries resources at FDM, and the possible effects of the bombing on these resources, would be of value at this time.

--- SENTENCE 186 ---
Another situation that may require attention is the status of the coral reefs and their associated fisheries on the few offshore banks and shoals that are being heavily fished in the EEZ at present.

--- SENTENCE 187 ---
This would include Penguin Bank in Hawaii, Galvez Bank on Guam, and Esmeralda Bank and the banks surrounding Farallon de Medinilla in CNMI (see above).

--- SENTENCE 188 ---
A more thorough assessment of the condition of these reefs, and their patterns of use, is required before management recommendations can be made for these areas.

--- SENTENCE 189 ---
A more critical issue is the mounting body of evidence that the coral reef resources in state and territorial waters in the region are being degraded and over-exploited.

--- SENTENCE 190 ---
Local government agencies, which are responsible for managing these resources, may need to increase the priority of allocating funds to protect these resources.

--- SENTENCE 191 ---
Another option may

be for the Council to consider establishing reefs in remote federal waters as reserves, offlimits to fishing, which may act as sources of larvae for the replenishment of some of the species that are heavily exploited on nearshore reefs.

--- SENTENCE 192 ---
It is also recommended that the need for management of coral reef resources in the EEZ be reassessed at regular intervals in the future, in case the situation changes.

--- SENTENCE 193 ---
Management measures should also be reconsidered at an earlier date if there is any evidence to suggest that substantial changes have occurred.

--- SENTENCE 194 ---
Such changes may include increased threats to coral reef health, or an increase in fishing pressure by either local or foreign interests.

--- SENTENCE 195 ---
The situation should also be reassessed if specialized fisheries become established in the area.

--- SENTENCE 196 ---
For example, if the live reef fish trade becomes established, since this trade has become a major fisheries management issue elsewhere in the Asia-Pacific Region.

--- SENTENCE 197 ---
Other aspects for further consideration include:

## 1.

--- SENTENCE 198 ---
Information Needs

This assessment was constrained by the general absence of good quality information on the condition of the reefs in the EEZ, and the total landings of coral reef resources in each state and territory.

--- SENTENCE 199 ---
Options to fill these important gaps in our knowledge should be considered, including identifying support for detailed resource assessments and the collection and analysis of improved fisheries statistics by local government agencies.

--- SENTENCE 200 ---
## 2. Overlap with Existing FMPs

Three of the Council's FMPs have the potential for some overlap with management of coral reef resources in the EEZ, possibly through a new FMP: the Bottomfish and Seamount Groundfish FMP, the Crustacean FMP and the Precious Corals FMP.

--- SENTENCE 201 ---
To clarify this issue, it would be important to identify which species, depths and gear types are covered by each plan.

--- SENTENCE 202 ---
Alternatively, an ecosystem-based FMP encompassing all of these fisheries may be a better management approach because the complexity of interactions among reef-associated species and shared habitat may make it difficult to manage these fisheries independently.

## 3.

--- SENTENCE 203 ---
Jurisdiction

The issue of jurisdiction over coral reef resources is complicated and unresolved in several areas in the Western Pacific Region.

--- SENTENCE 204 ---
It is recommended that this issue be addressed before proceeding with a management plan for the coral reef fisheries in the region.

--- SENTENCE 205 ---
## I. INTRODUCTION

Coral reefs are complex tropical ecosystems characterized by high biological diversity.

--- SENTENCE 206 ---
These reefs are an important natural resource in the U.S. Pacific Islands, since they provide the basis for coral reef fisheries and play an important role in tourism, recreation and shoreline protection (Richmond 1993a, Maragos et al. 1996, Birkeland 1997a, Grigg 1997a).

--- SENTENCE 207 ---
In many locations, coral reefs also play an integral role in the rich cultural heritage of the islands (Richmond 1993a, Green 1996a, Myers 1997, Grigg 1997a).

--- SENTENCE 208 ---
Unfortunately, coral reefs are being severely degraded by human activities in many locations around the world, including the Pacific Islands (Maragos et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 209 ---
In response to the concern about the global threat to coral reef resources, the International Coral Reef Initiative (ICRI) was established at the First Conference of the Parties of the Convention on Biological Diversity in 1994 (Maragos et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 210 ---
Since then, the United States has developed a domestic branch of the ICRI, the USCRI, which is aimed at the conservation and effective management of coral reef ecosystems in U.S. waters (Maragos et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 211 ---
This Initiative is based on cooperation among all levels of government, in partnership with non-governmental organizations, scientists, the private sector and the general public (Maragos et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 212 ---
The Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council (hereafter WPRFMC or the Council) is the policy-making organization for the management of fisheries in the Exclusive Economic Zone or EEZ (generally 3-200 nmi from shore) surrounding the U.S. Pacific Islands in the Western Pacific Region (Fig. 1), including:

- ▶ the State of Hawaii (Fig. 2),
- ▶ the Territory of American Samoa (Fig. 3),
- ▶ the Territory of Guam (Fig. 4),
- the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (hereafter CNMI: Fig. 4), and the unincorporated U.S. Pacific possessions collectively known as the Other U.S. Pacific Islands and Atolls (Johnston Atoll, Wake Atoll, Baker Island, Howland Island, Jarvis Island, Kingman Reef and Palmyra Atoll: Fig. 1).

--- SENTENCE 213 ---
In response to this increased international concern, the Council is interested in determining if there is a need for management of the coral reef resources within its jurisdiction.

--- SENTENCE 214 ---
The precedent for this has already been established, since three other U.S. Regional Fishery Management Councils (South Atlantic, Gulf and Caribbean Councils) already have fishery management plans (FMPs) to manage their coral reef resources.

--- SENTENCE 215 ---
The overall area of coral reef habitat in the Western Pacific Region is estimated to be 15,852 km<sup>2</sup> (<100 m depth), most of which is under WPRFMC fisheries management jurisdiction (10,762 km<sup>2</sup>: Hunter 1995).

--- SENTENCE 216 ---
However, legal jurisdiction for the fisheries surrounding many of the reefs and islands in the region is complex (Hunter 1995, Table 1) and a matter of some dispute among local and federal government agencies (see *Jurisdiction and Existing Management Regimes*).

--- SENTENCE 217 ---
In the opinion of legal counsel for WPRFMC (TM Beuttler, NOAA General Counsel, August 8, 1995), the Council has clear jurisdiction over fisheries management in the EEZ surrounding all

of the American Flag Pacific Islands (AFPI: Table 1).

--- SENTENCE 218 ---
WPRFMC also has jurisdiction, in some cases jointly with other federal agencies, up the shoreline (0-200 nmi from shore) on the other unicorporated U.S. possessions and on all of the islands in CNMI (T.M. Beuttler, NOAA General Counsel, August 8, 1995: Table 1).

--- SENTENCE 219 ---
However, the local government currently manages the coral reef resources in CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 220 ---
In order to determine if there is a need for management of the coral reef resources within its jurisdiction, WPRFMC requires three important pieces of information about its region:

- the extent and condition of the coral reef resources;
- ▶ the current patterns of utilization of these resources; and
- ▶ the existing management regimes in each location.

--- SENTENCE 221 ---
In 1995, the Council commissioned a preliminary report aimed at addressing these issues.

--- SENTENCE 222 ---
This report (Hunter 1995) includes a summary of:

- ▶ the overall area of coral reef habitat in the WPRFMC region;
- the extent and type of the coral reef resources in each the U.S. Pacific Islands;
- an overview of the general condition of these reefs and the human activities affecting reef health;
- the overall value of each of the fisheries in each of the islands; and
- the coral and "live rock" trade in the United States, including the Western Pacific Region.

--- SENTENCE 223 ---
For the purposes of this report, reef habitat was defined as "substratum adjacent to coastlines (or on shoals) from depths of 1-100 m that is primarily composed of hard-bottom" (Hunter 1995:

--- SENTENCE 224 ---
The aim of this study is to expand upon the Hunter report by providing a detailed assessment of:

- the condition of the coral reef resources in the U.S. Pacific Islands, focusing on five resources that have been identified as of particular interest to the Council (reef fishes, coral, "live rock", invertebrates, algae and non-consumptive resources),
- ▶ patterns of resource use in each of the U.S. Pacific Islands (including the most recent fisheries statistics available for each location),
- the degree to which these resources are already being managed by local government agencies; and
- special management issues which may be affecting coral reef resources in the region, including overfishing, habitat degradation and the status of specialized fisheries (live reef fish trade and the aquarium fish industry).

--- SENTENCE 225 ---
This report also considers management needs and identifies gaps in our knowledge where more information is required for the effective management of these resources.

--- SENTENCE 226 ---
<sup>&</sup>lt;sup>1</sup> "Live rock" is coral reef rock that is encrusted with an assortment of invertebrate and algal life.

--- SENTENCE 227 ---
Given the volume of information available on certain aspects of coral reefs in the region, this report is not intended to be a comprehensive review.

--- SENTENCE 228 ---
Instead, it is a synthesis of the existing knowledge of the region based on an overview of the existing literature (unpublished reports and papers published in scientific journals), and a series of interviews with knowledgeable local management agencies, non-government agencies, scientists, fishermen and other interested parties (e.g. divers).

--- SENTENCE 229 ---
Local specialists were also sub-contracted to synthesize some of the information (the condition of the resource and patterns of use) in each of three locations: Dr. Alan Friedlander in Hawaii, Mr. Robert Myers in Guam and Mr. John Gourley in CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 230 ---
The information contained in this review includes all of the information previously presented by these scientists contracted by WPRFMC to assess this issue, including the information contained in the reports prepared by Hunter (1995), Friedlander (1996), Myers (1997) and Gourley (1997).

#### II.

--- SENTENCE 247 ---
DESCRIPTION OF THE RESOURCE

The Western Pacific Region comprises a total of 106 recognized coral reefs with a combined area of 15,852 km² (Tables 2 & 3).

--- SENTENCE 248 ---
The majority of the coral reef area is located in federal waters in the EEZ (10,762 km²: Table 2), most of which is in the Northwest Hawaiian Islands (85%).

--- SENTENCE 249 ---
The remaining coral reef area located in the EEZ is in the Main Hawaiian Island (8%) and CNMI (5%), with only a small percentage (2%) located in Guam, American Samoa and the Other U.S. Pacific Islands.

--- SENTENCE 250 ---
However, Hunter (1995) advises that these figures should be interpreted as approximations only, because of the inherent difficulties in the method used to assess coral reef area (based on hydrological charts alone).

--- SENTENCE 251 ---
In some states and territories, the majority of the coral reef resources are in federal waters (Hunter 1995, Table 2).

--- SENTENCE 252 ---
In Hawaii, 71% of the reef area is located in federal waters, although the vast majority of this (91%) is located in the Northwest Hawaiian Islands.

--- SENTENCE 253 ---
The remainder is on Penguin Bank off Molokai, which is the most extensive shallow shelf area in the main Hawaiian Islands (Smith 1993), and around the small island of Kaula (Hunter 1995).

--- SENTENCE 254 ---
Similarly, the majority of the reef area in Guam (62%) is also in federal waters, including Galvez, Rota and Santa Rosa Banks and an unnamed shoal south of Guam (Hunter 1995).

--- SENTENCE 255 ---
The federal government's position is that its jurisdiction in the CNMI extends from the shoreline to 200 nmi, which includes all waters with coral reef.

--- SENTENCE 256 ---
The majority of these resources (92%) are located more than three miles from shore.

--- SENTENCE 257 ---
In contrast, only a small portion (13%) of the coral reef areas in the Other U.S. Pacific Islands (Johnston, Howland, Baker, Jarvis, Palmyra, Kingman Reef, Wake) lie in the EEZ 2-200 nmi from shore.

--- SENTENCE 258 ---
Similarly, only a very small proportion of the coral reefs in American Samoa (8%) lay within federal waters.

All known reef types are represented in 106 reefs recognized in the WPRFMC region (Hunter 1995, Table 3), including atoll, fringing, barrier/lagoon, submerged banks/shoals and non-

structural reef communities (sensu Maragos & Holthus in press).

--- SENTENCE 265 ---
Most of the reefs are banks or shoals (37%), non-structural reefs (25%) or fringing reefs (22%).

--- SENTENCE 266 ---
Only a few of the reefs are atolls (10%) or barrier/lagoon reefs (6%).

--- SENTENCE 267 ---
Each of the states or territories differ in the type of reefs that they contain (Hunter 1995, Table 3).

--- SENTENCE 268 ---
Most of the reefs in main Hawaiian Islands are large non-structural or fringing reefs as well as a few barrier reefs and banks or shoals.

--- SENTENCE 269 ---
In contrast, most of the reefs in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands are banks/shoals, although there are also a few atolls, non-structural reefs and fringing reefs.

--- SENTENCE 270 ---
Similarly, the reefs of CNMI tend to be mostly banks/shoals or non-structural reefs, although there are also some fringing and barrier/lagoon reefs.

--- SENTENCE 271 ---
American Samoa has mostly fringing reefs, with two remote atolls and two non-structural reefs.

--- SENTENCE 272 ---
Most of the reefs on Guam are a mixture of banks/shoals, barrier/lagoon reefs and fringing or non-structural reefs.

--- SENTENCE 273 ---
The Other U.S. Islands are either atolls or fringing reefs.

--- SENTENCE 274 ---
In contrast, there are no atolls in Guam, the Main Hawaiian Islands or CNMI.

The overall condition of the coral reef communities in each location are summarized below:

## 2.1 Coral Reef Communities

The condition of the coral reefs in the U. S. Pacific Islands varies greatly.

--- SENTENCE 278 ---
In general, reefs tend to be in poorer condition where they are close to major population centers, and in better condition in more remote locations.

--- SENTENCE 279 ---
As such, reefs tend to be in better condition in federal waters than in state or territorial waters, because reefs in federal waters tend to be further offshore.

--- SENTENCE 280 ---
## 2.1.1 American Samoa

The total coral reef area in American Samoa is relatively small (296 km²: Hunter 1995, Tables 2 & 4).

--- SENTENCE 281 ---
The majority of the reefs in American Samoa are in territorial waters (271 km²), with only a small amount located in federal waters (25 m²: Tables 2 & 4).

--- SENTENCE 282 ---
Most of the reefs in territorial waters are fringing reefs around volcanic islands (Table 3), including the main island of Tutuila (243 km²) and the smaller islands of the Manu'a Group (6.9 km²: Table 4, Fig. 3).

--- SENTENCE 283 ---
Other reef areas in territorial waters include the two remote atolls (10.3 km² at Rose and Swains) and two submerged banks off Tutuila (10 km² on Taema and Nafanua Banks: Table 4).

--- SENTENCE 284 ---
The limited amount of reef area that is located in federal waters is situated on submerged banks in federal waters east and west of Tutuila Island (25 km²: Table 4).

--- SENTENCE 285 ---
The structure and development of most of these reefs, except the submerged banks, has been well described in recent years (Maragos et al. 1994, Maragos 1994, Green 1996a, Green & Craig 1996).

--- SENTENCE 286 ---

--- SENTENCE 288 ---
The condition coral reef communities in territorial waters have also been well described by numerous quantitative and qualitative surveys over the last few years, including: Birkeland et al. 1987.

--- SENTENCE 289 ---
Hunter et al 1993; Maragos 1994; Maragos et al. 1994; Mundy 1996; Green 1996a; Green & Craig 1996; Green et al. in press; Green et al. ms).

--- SENTENCE 290 ---
In general, the reefs adjacent to human population centers (e.g. Tutuila Island) appear to be worse condition than those on less populated or unpopulated islands (e.g. the Manu'a Group and the two remote atolls: Green 1996a).

--- SENTENCE 291 ---
The reefs on the main island of Tutuila Island have been badly damaged by a combination of natural and anthropogenic disturbances in the last two decades.

--- SENTENCE 292 ---
These include a severe outbreak of the crown-of-thorns starfish in the 1970s, two major hurricanes in the last seven years (Hurricanes Ofa and Val in 1990 and 1991 respectively), and a mass coral bleaching event in 1994 (Maragos et al. 1994, Birkeland et al. 1996, Green 1996a).

--- SENTENCE 293 ---
In some locations (especially Pago Pago Harbor and Pala Lagoon), these reefs also appear to have been degraded by a combination of anthropogenic processes, including coastal construction, sedimentation,

eutrophication, chemical and solid waste pollution (Maragos et al. 1994, Green 1996a, Green et al. in press).

--- SENTENCE 294 ---
Long term monitoring of these reefs show that these disturbances have resulted in major changes to the coral and fish communities on the island over the last 20-80 years (Birkeland et al. 1996, Green et al. in press, Green et al. ms).

--- SENTENCE 295 ---
The rate of recovery of the coral reef communities on Tutuila appears to be quite variable.

--- SENTENCE 296 ---
The reefs in Fagatele Bay National Marine Sanctuary (FBNMS) and at most other locations are recovering well from these disturbances (Birkeland et al. 1987, 1994, 1996, Green 1996a, Green et al. ms).

--- SENTENCE 297 ---
In contrast, the reefs in Pago Pago Harbor and at several other locations around the island are not (Birkeland et al. 1987, 1994, 1996, Mundy 1996, Green et al. in press).

--- SENTENCE 298 ---
Differences in water quality among sites may be partly responsible for these differences among reefs.

--- SENTENCE 299 ---
For example, the reefs in good condition, including those at FBNMS, Leone, Fatumafuti and Vatia, appear to have good water quality (Mundy 1996, Green 1996a, Green et al. ms).

--- SENTENCE 300 ---
By comparison, the reefs that are in poor condition appear to have poor water quality, including high sediment loads and the presence of chemical pollutants (Maragos et al. 1994, Mundy 1996, Green 1996a, Green et al. in press).

--- SENTENCE 301 ---
Poor quality reefs include most of the reefs in Pago Pago Harbor and some reefs on the NW shore (Fagasa and Fagafue: Maragos et al. 1994, Mundy 1996, Green 1996a, Green et al. in press).

--- SENTENCE 302 ---
In general, the reefs on the other, less populated, islands appear to be in good condition (Green 1996a, Mundy 1996).

--- SENTENCE 303 ---
The small island of Aunu'u Island has suffered the same natural disturbances as Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 304 ---
However, they are relatively protected from anthropogenic effects, and they are recovering quickly from the hurricanes and are in excellent condition (Mundy 1996, Green 1996a).

--- SENTENCE 305 ---
The reefs of the Manu'a Islands (Ofu, Olosega and Ta'u) were severely damaged by Hurricane Tusi in 1987, but escaped major damage in the two more recent hurricanes (Green 1996a).

--- SENTENCE 306 ---
The starfish invasion in the 1970s and the recent coral bleaching event also affected these reefs, but the extent of the damage is unclear (Green 1996a).

--- SENTENCE 307 ---
Several studies over the last ten years have shown that the reefs of the Manu'a Group tend to be in better condition than those on Tutuila (Itano & Buckley 1988, Maragos et al. 1994, Mundy 1996, Green 1996a).

--- SENTENCE 308 ---
In fact, Green (1996a) and Mundy (1996) reported that some of the reefs in Manu'a were among the best surveyed in the archipelago, including reefs on Ofu (Asaga), Olosega (Sili and Olosega Village) and Ta'u (Lepula and Afuli).

--- SENTENCE 309 ---
The shallow lagoon in the National Park is also in particularly good condition (Hunter et al. 1993, Green 1996a, see Non-consumptive Resources).

--- SENTENCE 310 ---
In general, anthropogenic effects are less pronounced in the Manu'a Islands, because of the lower population on these islands.

--- SENTENCE 311 ---
However, the future of some of these reefs is currently threatened by road construction immediately adjacent to the shoreline on all three islands (Green & Mundy 1995, Green 1996a).

--- SENTENCE 312 ---
Intermittent, moderate to large infestations of the crown-of-thorns starfish may also threaten the condition of some of these reefs in future, especially on Ofu and Olosega (Zann 1992, Mundy 1996)

--- SENTENCE 313 ---
American Samoa has two remote atolls.

--- SENTENCE 314 ---
Rose Atoll is a National Wildlife Refuge, which UNEP/IUCN (1988) listed as one of the most pristine coral reefs in the world.

--- SENTENCE 315 ---
Rose Atoll is dominated by a lush growth of pink coralline algae (Mayor 1921, Maragos 1994), and coral cover and diversity are quite low relative to the other islands in American Samoa (Mayor 1921, Maragos 1994, Green 1996a).

--- SENTENCE 316 ---
However, this appears to be the normal condition for Rose, and Mayor (1921) suggested that it should be called a "lithothamnium atoll" rather than a coral atoll, because of the dominance of this alga.

--- SENTENCE 317 ---
Fish communities at Rose are in excellent condition and are characterized by a high density, and moderate to high species richness and biomass relative to the other islands (Green 1996a).

--- SENTENCE 318 ---
Rose Atoll is important refuge for giant clams (*Tridacna maxima*), which have been overfished throughout the rest of the Samoan Archipelago (Green & Craig 1996).

--- SENTENCE 319 ---
Unfortunately, the near pristine condition of Rose was compromised in 1993 when a fishing vessel ran aground on the southwest side of the atoll, spilling >100,000 gallons of diesel fuel onto the reef (USFWS 1997).

--- SENTENCE 320 ---
The grounding has had a dramatic impact on the coral reef communities on the southwest side of atoll (USFWS 1997, see *Pollution and Contamination*).

--- SENTENCE 321 ---
However, the rest of the atoll still appears to be in relatively good condition (Green 1996, pers.

--- SENTENCE 322 ---
Swains Island is a remote coral atoll that is geographically located in the Tokelau Group 370 km to the north of Tutuila (Green 1996a).

--- SENTENCE 323 ---
The reefs at Swains were devastated by a violent in storm in 1987 (D. Itano unpubl.

--- SENTENCE 324 ---
data), but they have largely recovered from this event and are now in an excellent condition (Green 1996a).

--- SENTENCE 325 ---
The lush condition of these reefs, combined with excellent water clarity and steep drop-offs, make the reefs of Swains Island some of the most spectacular in the Territory (Green 1996a).

--- SENTENCE 326 ---
Only two small areas of reef (total area=25 km²) are located in federal waters in American Samoa (Hunter 1995).

--- SENTENCE 327 ---
Both of these areas are located off Tutuila: 3 to 5 nmi off Cape Taputapu in the west and Cape Matatula in the east (Hunter 1995).

--- SENTENCE 328 ---
Virtually nothing is known about the condition of these reefs, except that navigational charts indicate that there is coral present at depths of 60-120 m (Hunter 1995).

## 2.1.2 CNMI

CNMI encompasses 14 islands stretching over a distance of 400 nmi (Gourley 1997, Fig. 4).

--- SENTENCE 329 ---
These islands can be divided into two sections (Eldredge 1983, Asakura et al. 1994a): the southern raised limestone islands (including Saipan, Tinian, Rota, Aguijan and Farallon de Medinilla) and the northern volcanic islands (including Anatahan, Sarigan, Guguan, Alamagan, Pagan, Agrihan, Asuncion, Maug and Uracas).

--- SENTENCE 330 ---
Over 99.5% of the total population (58,846 in 1995: see Gourley 1997) live on the three southern islands of Saipan, Tinian and Rota, with 89% living on Saipan alone (Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 331 ---
In addition to the islands, there are numerous submerged seamounts and unnamed shoals in CNMI (Eldredge 1983, Hunter 1995, Fig. 4).

--- SENTENCE 332 ---
The submerged seamounts run in a north-direction,

approximately parallel to the main islands and 120-180 nmi to the west (Gourley 1997, Polovina et al. 1985).

--- SENTENCE 333 ---
These seamounts include Pathfinder Reef, Arakane Reef, and Banks A, C and D (Polovina et al. 1985, Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 334 ---
Hunter (1995) also identified 12 shoals in the Commonwealth including: seven in the southern islands (one west of Saipan, two west of Tinian, one west of Rota, and three north of Farallon de Medinilla); and five in the northern islands (one west of Pagan, three west of Alamagan, and one west of Guguan).

--- SENTENCE 335 ---
However, Gourley (1997) noted that this list was incomplete, since there are other shoals in the Commonwealth that were not listed by Hunter (1995), including one south of Aguijan, one north of Saipan, one west of Saipan, and one between Sarigan and Guguan.

--- SENTENCE 336 ---
The total coral reef area in CNMI is 579 km<sup>2</sup>, of which 534 km<sup>2</sup> is situated in the EEZ (>3 nmi from shore: Hunter 1995, Tables 2 & 5).

--- SENTENCE 337 ---
Most of the reefs in nearshore waters are located on the southern islands of Saipan, Tinian and Rota (64%: Table 5), with the remainder situated on the northern islands (especially Pagan, Agrihan and Alamagan: Table 5).

--- SENTENCE 338 ---
The majority of the reef area in the EEZ (58%) is located on the submerged bank at Farallon de Medinilla (Table 5), and the rest is located on submerged banks and seamounts (Table 5).

--- SENTENCE 339 ---
The southern islands in CNMI are relatively old, and support a variety of marine habitat types (>35 million years:

--- SENTENCE 340 ---
Asakura et al. 1994a).

--- SENTENCE 341 ---
The coral reef resources of Saipan include fringing reefs, inshore and offshore patch reefs, and a well-developed barrier reef-lagoon system along most of the leeward coast (Eldredge 1983, Donaldson 1995, Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 342 ---
Saipan Lagoon also comprises some large areas of well-developed seagrass beds, as well as a small area of mangroves (Donaldson 1995, Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 343 ---
The reefs of Rota, Tinian and Aguijan are less well developed than those on Saipan, and are generally restricted to small fringing reef systems (Eldredge 1983, Donaldson 1995, Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 344 ---
A recent study of the reefs adjacent to beaches on Tinian reported that coral reefs are present around much of the island and, in general, reefs on the eastern (leeward) coastline are better developed and have greater species diversity than those on the western coast (see PSDA 1997).

--- SENTENCE 345 ---
Rota also has some well developed reefs, especially in Sasanhaya Bay on the south side, as well as some offshore reefs on north and west sides of the island (Donaldson 1995, PSDA 1997).

--- SENTENCE 346 ---
Farallon de Medinilla (FDM) is an uninhabited island that has been used as a military bombardment range for the last 26 years (Eldredge 1983, PSDA 1997).

--- SENTENCE 347 ---
There is no fringing reef or shallow coastal zone at FDM, since deepwater surrounds much of the island and the submarine slope appear to be very steep (PSDA 1997).

--- SENTENCE 348 ---
The combination of this vertical profile and wave action on the windward side of the island probably explains the limited coral reef biota in shallow water on that side (PSDA 1997).

--- SENTENCE 349 ---
As such, marine resources are mostly concentrated on the leeward side of the island, where the substrate drops gradually seaward (PSDA 1997).

--- SENTENCE 350 ---
Farallon de Medinilla also supports an extensive shallow bank a mile north of the island (about 18 m deep: PSDA 1997), which is the most extensive coral reef area in the Mariana Islands (311 km²: see Hunter 1995).

--- SENTENCE 351 ---

--- SENTENCE 365 ---
In contrast, the northern islands are relatively young (1-1.5 myp) and include five active volcanoes on the islands of Pagan (which erupted in 1981), Guguan, Asuncion, Agrihan and Uracas (Asakura et al. 1994a).

--- SENTENCE 366 ---
In general, reef development is poor or non-existent on the northern islands (Eldredge 1983).

--- SENTENCE 367 ---
Most of the reefs that do exist tend to be narrow, rocky reefs on steep slopes, with coral communities growing on volcanic substrata and little true coral reef development (Eldredge et al. 1977a, Eldredge 1983, Donaldson 1995, Birkeland 1997b).

--- SENTENCE 368 ---
However there are a few small "embryonic" or "apron" reefs on these islands, which may have some reef formation but do not reach sea level (Birkeland 1997b).

--- SENTENCE 369 ---
These include areas at depths of >25m at western Anatahan, southern Sarigan, and parts of Pagan (Donaldson et al. 1994,

Donaldson 1995).

--- SENTENCE 370 ---
Eldredge et al. (1977a) also reported a well-developed fringing reef on the seaward side of West Island on Maug.

--- SENTENCE 371 ---
These differences in the development of reefs throughout the Marianas appears to be related to the age and geology of the islands, since coral growth is just as vigorous in both the north and south (Birkeland 1997b).

--- SENTENCE 372 ---
For example, geological faulting of large areas in the older Southern Marianas (e.g. west coast of Saipan), have created large, oblique, shallow-water surfaces, which has allowed for extensive reef growth and the development of reef flats and lagoons over time (Birkeland 1997b).

--- SENTENCE 373 ---
In contrast, the islands in the north are younger and quite vertical in profile, which does not provide the basis for extensive reef development (Birkeland 1997b).

--- SENTENCE 374 ---
The condition of individual reefs on Saipan, Rota, Tinian and some of the northern islands have been assessed in numerous environmental impact studies over the last twenty years (see University of Guam Marine Laboratory Technical Report Series, Eldredge 1987, in prep.).

--- SENTENCE 375 ---
These reports contain detailed quantitative assessments of reefs in some locations.

--- SENTENCE 376 ---
However, most are not useful for this assessment because they are outdated, or the data are not summarized in a usable format.

--- SENTENCE 377 ---
But these reports may be of historical value and are listed in the bibliography for future reference.

--- SENTENCE 378 ---
However, these reports do provide some valuable background information on the reefs over time.

--- SENTENCE 379 ---
For example, these reports note the some of the islands in southern CNMI (Saipan, Tinian, Rota and Aguijan) have experienced at least one mass outbreak of the corallivorous crown-of-thorns starfish in the last few decades (Chesher 1969, Marsh & Tsuda 1973, Jones et al. 1974; see Duenas & Swavely 1985).

--- SENTENCE 380 ---
This outbreak occurred in the late 1960's at the same time as the starfish invasion on Guam (Chesher 1969, Marsh & Tsuda 1973), and is known to have caused extensive damage to some of the reefs on Saipan and elsewhere in CNMI (e.g. Tinian: Jones et al. 1974, see Duenas & Swavely 1985).

--- SENTENCE 381 ---
Low to moderate numbers of starfish have also been assumed to be responsible for substantial coral mortality on some reefs on Saipan over the last two decades.

--- SENTENCE 382 ---
This includes areas in Saipan Lagoon (see Duenas & Swavely 1985, Richmond & Matson 1986), the Obyan-Naftan area (Randall et al. 1988), and Laulau Bay (see PBEC 1984, Randall et al. 1991).

--- SENTENCE 383 ---
However, the starfish do not appear to be abundant on Saipan at present, and local divers report that starfish are only seen occasionally at the primary dive sites (e.g. Obyan and Laulau Bay: J. Comfort pers.

--- SENTENCE 384 ---
Starfish outbreaks have also been recorded on the other islands.

--- SENTENCE 385 ---
For example, divers have observed occasional, small-scale outbreaks on Rota since the 1980s (Mark Michael pers.

--- SENTENCE 386 ---
There have also been reports of starfish causing damage to reefs on the northern islands of CNMI, including Maug (Eldredge et al. 1977a in Irimura et al. 1994) and Alamagan (Eldredge 1983).

--- SENTENCE 387 ---
The coral reefs in CNMI are also likely to have experienced some damage from the frequent typhoons in the area (see *Guam* below).

--- SENTENCE 388 ---
In addition, the reefs in some locations appear to have been affected by human activities, including overfishing, sedimentation and nutrient loading (see below).

--- SENTENCE 389 ---
Several, localized coral bleaching events have also been noticed in recent years, which may be related to human activities in the area (see *Sedimentation*).

--- SENTENCE 390 ---
Best available information suggests that the current condition of the coral reefs in the southern islands of CNMI is quite variable.

--- SENTENCE 391 ---
Most appear to be in good condition, except in some heavily populated areas where the reefs have been degraded by human activities (e.g. overfishing, sedimentation: J. Gourley pers.

--- SENTENCE 392 ---
The major focus for concern are the reefs in Saipan Lagoon, since this area encompasses nearly all of the Commonwealth's population, tourism industry, commercial activity, subsistence fishing, and water-oriented recreation (see Duenas & Swavely 1985).

--- SENTENCE 393 ---
Local opinion is that many of the reefs in Saipan Lagoon have been degraded by human activities (DFW, DEQ and CRM personnel pers.

--- SENTENCE 394 ---
comm.), including some nearshore patch reefs in Garapan (J. Gourley pers.

--- SENTENCE 395 ---
comm., see *Sedimentation*) and the reefs immediately adjacent to Managaha Island (CRM 1996, see *Nutrient Loading*).

--- SENTENCE 396 ---
In particular, overfishing is considered to be a major problem in Saipan Lagoon (see *Overfishing*).

--- SENTENCE 397 ---
Parts of Laulau Bay on the eastcoast of Saipan also appear to have been degraded by human activities in recent years (see *Sedimentation*).

--- SENTENCE 398 ---
Most of the relatively inaccessible reefs on Saipan are in good condition, including those on the northwest (e.g. Wing Beach and Bonsai) and eastern sides (e.g. Forbidden Island: J. Comfort and J. Taman pers.

--- SENTENCE 399 ---
In addition, some of the more accessible reefs on Saipan are also still in reasonably good condition (J. Comfort pers.

--- SENTENCE 400 ---
These include the reefs from Obyan to Naftan (southeast side), at the Grotto (northeast side), and in the vicinity of Managaha Island in Saipan Lagoon (J. Comfort and DFW personnel pers.

--- SENTENCE 401 ---
Most of the reefs on Tinian and Rota are also in good condition (J. Gourley, S. Burr and J. Taman pers.

--- SENTENCE 402 ---
comm.), especially in Sasanhaya Bay on Rota (but see *Military Activities*).

--- SENTENCE 403 ---
In general, it appears that the reefs in the northern islands are also in good condition, because of their isolation from human population centers (Birkeland 1997b).

--- SENTENCE 404 ---
The exceptions are localized areas that may have been affected by volcanic or military activities (e.g. Pagan and Farallon de Medinilla: see *Geologic Activities* and *Military Activities*).

--- SENTENCE 405 ---
Coral reefs located in the EEZ include numerous banks, shoals and seamounts (Hunter 1995, Table 5).

--- SENTENCE 406 ---
The largest is the extensive bank at Farallon de Medinilla.

--- SENTENCE 407 ---
The condition of this reef is largely unknown, since the area has been used as a military bombing target since 1971 (Eldredge 1983).

--- SENTENCE 408 ---
However, biologists from NMFS, USFWS, and DFW recently completed a brief assessment of the area (see *Military Activities*).

--- SENTENCE 409 ---
They reported that the reefs appeared to be in reasonably good condition with high coral cover in some locations (70-80%), despite the obvious effects of the bombing (J. Naughton pers.

--- SENTENCE 410 ---
comm., see *Military Activities*).

--- SENTENCE 411 ---
However, the

abundance of large reef fish appeared low, especially *Lethrinus rubrioperculatus* which is targeted by local fishermen (J. Naughton pers.

--- SENTENCE 412 ---
comm., see *Patterns of Utilization*).

--- SENTENCE 413 ---
Little is known about the condition of the other reefs in the EEZ.

--- SENTENCE 414 ---
Some are located in the main chain of islands, and the ones closest to human population centers have been reported to be overfished (e.g. Esmeralda: C. La Plante, J. Gourley and J. Taman pers.

--- SENTENCE 415 ---
The rest are located in the chain of submerged shoals and seamounts situated 120-180 nmi west of the main islands (Hunter 1995, Table 5).

--- SENTENCE 416 ---
At present, there is virtually no information available on the condition of these reefs, because they are so remote.

--- SENTENCE 417 ---
However, anecdotal reports suggest that they are probably still in good condition, because of they are rarely visited by scientists or local fishermen (J. Polovina, R. Sakomoto and E. Poppe pers comm.).

--- SENTENCE 418 ---
However, the degree of poaching by foreign vessels is unknown (DFW personnel pers.

--- SENTENCE 419 ---
Guam

Approximately 50% of Guam's 153 km shoreline is surrounded by well developed coral reefs (Randall & Myers 1983, Myers 1997).

--- SENTENCE 420 ---
Most of the reefs are fringing reefs (up to 600m wide), except for the broad barrier reef enclosing the shallow Cocos Lagoon at the southwest tip of the island (Eldredge 1983, Randall & Myers 1983).

--- SENTENCE 421 ---
A raised barrier reef (Cabras Island), a greatly disturbed barrier reef (Luminao Reef) and a coral bank (Calalan Bank), enclose the deep lagoon of Apra Harbor (Randall & Myers 1983).

--- SENTENCE 422 ---
Patch reefs are also associated with Anae Island on the southwest coast and at Pugua Patch Reef (or Double Reef) on the northwest coast (Randall & Myers 1983).

--- SENTENCE 423 ---
All of the reef flats, lagoons, patch reefs and outer reef slopes surrounding Guam are located within territorial waters (Hunter 1995, Myers 1997).

--- SENTENCE 424 ---
Deepwater banks are located at several locations around the island, four of which are located in federal waters (Rota Bank to the north and Galvez, Santa Rosa and White Tuna Bank to the south (Donaldson 1995, Hunter 1995, Myers 1997, Fig. 4).

--- SENTENCE 425 ---
These offshore submerged banks, with a minimum depth ranging from 5-60m, represent the only coral reefs within federal waters in Guam (Hunter 1995, Myers 1997).

--- SENTENCE 426 ---
Recent calculations by Hunter (1995, Table 2) from National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) charts suggest that the total reef area in Guam (≤ 100 m depth) is small (179 km²), most of which (110 km² or 62%) is located within federal waters (Tables 2 & 6).

--- SENTENCE 427 ---
Most of the reefs located in territorial waters are located on the island of Guam, while all of the reefs in federal waters are located on the offshore banks (Table 6, Fig. 4).

--- SENTENCE 428 ---
At present, the South Pacific Commission (SPC) is nearing completion of a detailed bathymetric survey of Guam's reefs and banks, which should provide more precise information on reef area by depth in Guam in future (G. Davis pers.

--- SENTENCE 429 ---
Local scientists have reported a substantial decline in coral reef health on Guam over the last two decades, and most of the reefs now appear to be in poor condition (R. Richmond and C. Birkeland pers.

--- SENTENCE 430 ---
For example, coral cover and species diversity have both decreased dramatically at many locations (G. Davis, R. Richmond and C. Birkeland pers.

--- SENTENCE 431 ---
In contrast, algal communities have thrived and become dominant, and some aggressive coral species, which do well under disturbed conditions, have increased in abundance (e.g. *Porites rus*:

R. Richmond pers.

--- SENTENCE 432 ---
These changes in the coral reef communities on Guam are due a combination of natural and anthropogenic disturbances on the island (Birkeland 1997b).

Typhoons are frequent on Guam (up to five major typhoons per year:

--- SENTENCE 441 ---
Eldredge 1983, USDA 1995, Birkeland 1997b), which cause some damage to the reefs (Randall & Eldredge 1977, Birkeland 1997b).

--- SENTENCE 442 ---
However, the reefs on Guam tend to experience less physical damage from these storms than is the case in other areas, because corals in exposed locations are "adapted" to these rough conditions and grow in low profile growth forms (Randall & Eldredge 1977, Birkeland 1997b).

--- SENTENCE 443 ---
As such, severe typhoon damage to the reefs on Guam tends to be localized in areas that are usually protected from heavy wave action by the shape of the coastline (Birkeland 1997b).

--- SENTENCE 444 ---
Several outbreaks of the crown-of-thorns starfish have also occurred on Guam over the last few decades (Birkeland 1997b).

--- SENTENCE 445 ---
One outbreak in the 1960s, caused severe catastrophic mortality (90%) of reef slope corals along 38 km of Guam's northwest coast (Randall 1971, 1973, Colgan 1981, 1982, Chesher 1986).

--- SENTENCE 446 ---
However by 1981, the reefs had started to recover from the starfish invasion and coral cover was high again (65%: Colgan 1987).

--- SENTENCE 447 ---
Occasional earthquakes and El Nino events have also been known to cause substantial damage to the reefs on Guam (Birkeland 1997b).

--- SENTENCE 448 ---
However, the biggest threat to Guam's reefs appears to be from anthropogenic effects, including overfishing and habitat degradation due to poor land use practices, urbanization and development (Myers 1997, see Habitat Degradation).

--- SENTENCE 449 ---
Sedimentation and overfishing are probably the most serious problems causing coral reef degradation on Guam (Myers 1997, Birkeland 1997b, see Overfishing and Sedimentation).

--- SENTENCE 450 ---
For example, Birkeland (1997b) reported that the rates of coral replenishment have been substantially reduced on Guam over the last 20 years, possibly as a result of increased sedimentation and the overfishing of herbivores (Birkeland 1997b).

--- SENTENCE 451 ---
As a result of the loss of living cover and the lack of replenishment of these reefs, coral cover on the island has declined substantially over time (Birkeland 1997b).

--- SENTENCE 452 ---
This effect has been most pronounced on the reef slopes, and coral cover is still reasonably high in some places on the reef flat (Birkeland 1997b).

--- SENTENCE 453 ---
Other anthropogenic impacts that may have affected coral reef health on Guam include industrial pollution, non-point source pollution, oil spills, sewage and coastal construction (Myers 1997).

--- SENTENCE 454 ---
The coral reefs around Guam have been the subject of a multitude of coral reef assessments over the last 30 years, especially during the 1970s.

--- SENTENCE 455 ---
Most of these surveys were done as environmental impact assessments related to coastal construction, industry and sewage on the island (see University of Guam Marine Laboratory Technical Report Series, Eldredge 1987, in prep.).

--- SENTENCE 456 ---
These reports provide a brief insight into the condition of the reefs resources at the time of the study (often prior to an impact).

--- SENTENCE 457 ---
However, many of these reports are of little value in assessing the condition of the resources at present, since they were done so long ago and conditions have now changed in most locations.

--- SENTENCE 458 ---
Current opinion is that coral reef health varies around the island of Guam.

--- SENTENCE 459 ---
In general many of the reefs on the southern part of the island tend to be in poor condition, because of the high population base, extensive coastal development, good reef access, and high runoff of terrigenous sediments onto the reefs from large rivers (Myers 1997).

--- SENTENCE 460 ---
One example is the reef between Facpi Point and Umatac on the southwest side of the island, which has been buried by sediment in recent years (R. Myers, R. Richmond and S. Amesbury pers.

--- SENTENCE 461 ---
By contrast, the reefs on the northern part of the island (e.g. Ritidian Point and Pati Point) tend to be in better condition because there are fewer people, less development, less access to the reef, and no major rivers (R. Myers, C. Birkeland, S. Amesbury and R. Sakomoto pers.

--- SENTENCE 462 ---
Virtually nothing is known of the coral reef resources on the banks in federal waters in Guam (Myers 1997), since they are in remote locations and difficult to access (DAWR personnel pers.

--- SENTENCE 463 ---
The small amount of information that is available is based on anecdotal observations by scientists and fishermen, who have made one or more dives on the banks (e.g. C. Birkeland and E. Poppe Jnr.

--- SENTENCE 464 ---
In general, Rota, Santa Rosa and White Tuna Banks (= unnamed shoal south of Guam) are thought to be in good condition, while Galvez is thought to be in worse condition, because it is closer to Guam and more heavily fished (J. Cruz pers.

--- SENTENCE 465 ---
Hawaii

Coral reefs in the Hawaii constitute the vast majority of coral reef area in the WPRFMC region (89%: Hunter 1995, Table 2).

--- SENTENCE 466 ---
Most of the reef area in Hawaii is located in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands (82%), while the remainder is located in the Main Hawaiian Islands (Table 7, Fig. 2).

--- SENTENCE 467 ---
Of the reefs in Main Hawaiian Islands (MHI), 35% is located in federal waters 3-200 nmi from shore (most of Penguin Bank on Molokai and some of Kaula Rock: Hunter 1995, Table 7, Fig.2).

--- SENTENCE 468 ---
In contrast, 79% of the reefs in the Northwest Hawaiian Islands (NWHI) are located in federal waters (Table 7).

--- SENTENCE 469 ---
Collectively, the reefs in federal waters in Hawaii comprise 93% of the reef area under federal jurisdiction in the region (8% and 85% in MHI and NWHI respectively: see Table 2).

--- SENTENCE 470 ---
The MHI represent the younger portion of the Hawaiian Archipelago, and they have less well-developed fringing reefs that have not subsided as far below sea level as those in the NWHI (Smith 1993).

--- SENTENCE 471 ---
The coral reefs of the MHI were mapped extensively in the 1970s and 1980s

(AECOS, Inc. 1979a,b,c, 1981, 1982; Maragos & Elliott 1985), and have been surveyed intermittently ever since.
