--- SENTENCE 1761 ---
This study has found that many of the reefs are comprised of calcareous algae with little live coral, and in some cases, extensive algal beds (such as at Brooks Bank and Necker: F. Parrish pers.

--- SENTENCE 1762 ---
However, some of the reefs have good coral cover, including Frigate Shoals, Laysan, Lisianski and Maro Reef (F. Parrish pers.

--- SENTENCE 1763 ---
French Frigate Shoals has the best coral cover, with high cover of *Acropora* species in places, especially in the southeastern end (F. Parrish pers.

--- SENTENCE 1764 ---
There is also a fair amount of coral at Pearl and Hermes Atoll (mostly *Porites compressa* and *P. lobata*: F. Parrish per.

--- SENTENCE 1765 ---
Coral cover is also high in patches at Laysan, Lisianksi and Maro Reef, although there tends to be less coral than at French Frigate Shoals and Pearl and Hermes Atoll, and these reefs tend to be dominated by calcareous reef areas.

--- SENTENCE 1766 ---
In the NWHI, coral cover has also been recorded to vary among habitats from 6% in the lagoon to 17% on the reef flat at French Frigate Shoals (Atkinson & Grigg 1984 in Hunter 1995).

--- SENTENCE 1767 ---
Similarly, DeMartini et al. (1994 in Hunter 1995) found that the outer barrier reef at Midway Atoll comprised primarily dead coral rock (>90% cover), while live coral cover was high (30-70%) inside the reef due to the abundance of *Montipora* microatolls.

--- SENTENCE 1768 ---
However, F. Parrish (pers.

comm.) noted that the corals inside the reef at Midway are often suffocated by the highly mobile sand banks in the lagoon (F. Parrish pers.

--- SENTENCE 1769 ---
Live rock resources are also available in the NWHI, although they tend to be limited to shallow areas on the atolls and a few of the banks.

--- SENTENCE 1770 ---
However, these resources are mostly inaccessible because they are hard to remove and frequently buried by mobile sand banks (F. Parrish pers.

--- SENTENCE 1771 ---
Live rock resources are probably not available on most of the other banks, because there is not much loose material lying around (F. Parrish pers.

--- SENTENCE 1772 ---
However, there is potential to "grow" live rock in some of these areas, if the rocks are transplanted there (F. Parrish pers.

--- SENTENCE 1773 ---
Although, such an industry would be fraught with difficulties because of the frequent storms and the distance to major population centers.

--- SENTENCE 1774 ---
At present, no information is available on the status of the coral communities in federal waters in the Main Hawaiian Islands.

--- SENTENCE 1775 ---
## 2.3.4 Other U.S. Pacific Islands

Very little is known of the coral resources on most of the Other U.S. Pacific Islands, although the region is known to support 20 to 30 coral genera (Veron 1993, USFWS 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1776 ---
Almost all of the available information is for Johnston Atoll, where a number of surveys have been done over the last 30 years.

--- SENTENCE 1777 ---
A total of 33 coral species have been recorded at Johnston Atoll (Maragos & Jokiel 1986).

--- SENTENCE 1778 ---
Factors contributing to the low number of species include the atoll's remoteness, small size and unfavorable conditions for recruitment from the southwest Pacific (Maragos & Jokiel 1986).

--- SENTENCE 1779 ---
While most of the coral species found at Johnston are also found in Hawaii, the dominant coral, *Acropora cytherea*, is rare in the MHI and shows a restricted distribution in the NWHI (Maragos and Jokiel 1986, Maragos 1995).

--- SENTENCE 1780 ---
*A. cytherea* is responsible for some of the highest areal cover on the atoll (see below), which provides three-dimensional habitat for fish and invertebrates (Cooke 1986).

--- SENTENCE 1781 ---
This suggests that while the coral community at Johnston is derived primarily from Hawaii, it may be more ecologically similar to atolls to the south and west where various *Acropora* species are also dominant (Cooke 1986).

--- SENTENCE 1782 ---
Some coral communities were destroyed by dredging in 1963-64 in some areas on Johnston Atoll, but considerable recovery of the dredged areas seems to have taken place (Brock et al. 1965, 1966 in Cooke 1986, Irons et al. 1984, see below).

--- SENTENCE 1783 ---
Elsewhere, the coral communities are virtually untouched (Brock et al. 1965, 1966 in Cooke 1986).

--- SENTENCE 1784 ---
Despite the low species diversity, coral cover at Johnston is extremely high (Cook 1986, Maragos & Jokiel 1986), ranging from 60-100% (Brock et al. 1965 in Hunter 1995, see below).

--- SENTENCE 1785 ---
More detailed information is available on the coral communities on Johnston Atoll, based on a resource survey done in 1984 (Irons et al. 1984).

--- SENTENCE 1786 ---
Irons et al. (1984) surveyed 113 sites at Johnston.

--- SENTENCE 1787 ---
On the basis of this survey, Irons et al. (1984) divided the shallow-water reefs on the

atoll into 12 distinctive zones or "ecotypes".

--- SENTENCE 1788 ---
Each "ecotype" was distinguished by distinctive physical characteristics and coral communities as follows (Irons et al. 1984):

Zone 1: This zone includes the shorelines and shallow nearshore waters (< 9m) surrounding the four islands, most of which have been highly disturbed by dredging, spoiling and shoreline construction.

--- SENTENCE 1789 ---
This zone was dominated by rubble with little live coral cover (mostly <20%), and the most abundant coral was *Montipora* spp.

--- SENTENCE 1790 ---
Zone 2: This zone consists of all the dredged channels.

--- SENTENCE 1791 ---
It has been highly disturbed, but recovery seems to be good along the sides and along the bottoms in some areas.

--- SENTENCE 1792 ---
There is great variability among channels.

--- SENTENCE 1793 ---
All of the channels have a fair amount of coral growth on the sides (75-90%), except for the west side of the East Channel.

--- SENTENCE 1794 ---
The shallower channels have more growth on the bottom than the deeper channels, because they have harder substrate.

--- SENTENCE 1795 ---
Visibility is good in most areas, and the channels are relatively deep (max. depth 15 m).

--- SENTENCE 1796 ---
The dominant coral is *Montipora* species.

--- SENTENCE 1797 ---
Zone 3: This zone extends along the northern, ocean side of the barrier reef immediately seaward of the breaker zone, and ranges in depth from the surface to 100s of feet.

--- SENTENCE 1798 ---
This area receives heavy wave action, and the substrate is low, eroded rock with little live coral cover (<20%).

--- SENTENCE 1799 ---
*Millepora tenera* is the dominant coral.

--- SENTENCE 1800 ---
Zone 4: This zone is the top of the barrier reef, and is shallow and characterized by strong wave action and surge.

--- SENTENCE 1801 ---
Most of the zone is a broad, flat-topped ridge with some gullies and holes in it.

--- SENTENCE 1802 ---
There is a fair amount of live coral growth, depending on how often the area is awash.

--- SENTENCE 1803 ---
The dominant coral is *Millepora tenera*.

--- SENTENCE 1804 ---
Zone 5: This zone is a shallow (<9m), narrow band just inside the barrier reef that extends from west of the West Channel near Johnston Island to east of Donovan's Reef in the northeast.

--- SENTENCE 1805 ---
The area is characterized by rolling flats and large sand areas, and there is a rubble slope close to the barrier reef.

--- SENTENCE 1806 ---
Live coral cover is high (>50%), and dominated by *Acropora* species.

--- SENTENCE 1807 ---
Zone 6: This zone is directly north of Johnston Island and Sand Island (<11m deep), but does not include the dredged channels.

--- SENTENCE 1808 ---
Live coral cover is very high (>75%), and *Montipora* species dominate.

--- SENTENCE 1809 ---
Zone 7: This zone is directly south of Zone 5 (depth 9-14m), extending from west of Akau Island to east of Donovan's Reef.

--- SENTENCE 1810 ---
Live coral cover is very high (mostly > 80%), and dominated by *Montipora* species.

--- SENTENCE 1811 ---
Zone 8: This is the most extensive zone of the atoll, and is a broad band extending from south of Sand and Hikina Islands to the eastern edge of the atoll.

--- SENTENCE 1812 ---
Coral cover is high (>60%) in most locations, and *Montipora* species dominate.

--- SENTENCE 1813 ---
Depth ranges from 9-15 m.

Zone 9: This zone is a band south of Zone 8, extending from the East Channel edge along the southeastern edge of the atoll.

--- SENTENCE 1814 ---
Coral cover is sparse (<50%), and dominated by *Montipora* species.

--- SENTENCE 1815 ---
This is the deepest zone on the atoll, ranging from 15-20m.

Zone 10: This is a small zone to the West of the West Channel between the West Camera Stand and the barrier reef (depth < 9m).

--- SENTENCE 1816 ---
Coral cover is very high (>70%), and dominated by *Montipora* species.

--- SENTENCE 1817 ---
Zone 11: This zone covers the remainder of the western end of the atoll, extending from the West Channel.

--- SENTENCE 1818 ---
Coral cover is very high (mostly >70%), and characterized by rolling hills of Acropora cytherea.

--- SENTENCE 1819 ---
Maximum depth is 11m.

Zone 12:

--- SENTENCE 1820 ---
This zone is directly south of Johnston Island extending from the West Channel to the East Channel.

--- SENTENCE 1821 ---
Coral cover is very high (mostly >70%), and dominated by *Montipora* species.

--- SENTENCE 1822 ---
This zone is fairly deep, ranging from 8-18 m.

Approximately 13 of the 113 sites surveyed by Irons et al. (1984) at Johnston Atoll appear to be in federal waters, since they were located >3 nmi from the islands.

--- SENTENCE 1823 ---
All of these sites were located in Zones 8 and 9.

--- SENTENCE 1824 ---
As such, the coral communities in federal waters at Johnston ranged from high coral cover in some locations (>60% in Zone 8: see above) to sparse cover in others (<50% in Zone 9: see above).

--- SENTENCE 1825 ---
The dominant corals in federal waters appear to be *Montipora* species (*M. patula/verrilli* and *M. verrucosa*), *Acropora* species (*Acropora cytherea* and *A.* sp.

--- SENTENCE 1826 ---
"A") and *Pavona* species (*P. duerdeni* and *P. maldivensis*: Irons et al. 1984).

--- SENTENCE 1827 ---
(Note: *M. verrucosa* is now considered a junior synonym for *M. capitata* (Maragos 1995).

--- SENTENCE 1828 ---
No information is available on the coral communities within federal waters on the other atolls, although the fringing reef at Jarvis Island has been reported to have a healthy coral community (USFWS Biological Summary).

--- SENTENCE 1829 ---
Similarly, the coral reefs of Palmyra are considered to be spectacular and support large coral populations (USFWS 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1830 ---
Coral reefs and corals were briefly surveyed at Palmyra by Maragos (1979a, 1988) and at Wake by Maragos (1979b, unpublished).

--- SENTENCE 1831 ---
A total of 93 species and 35 genera of corals were reported from Palmyra, and about 30 species of coral were reported from Wake.

--- SENTENCE 1832 ---
The Palmyra totals are roughly twice those of Hawaii and three times those of Johnston some 1600 km and 1000 km north of Johnston.

--- SENTENCE 1833 ---
However, these values are comparable to what has been reported at nearby Christmas and Fanning atolls.

--- SENTENCE 1834 ---
Although 1988 surveys revealed that reefs in the lagoon have recovered only minimally from previous WWII-era military construction (see Dawson 1959).

--- SENTENCE 1835 ---
open lagoon and terrace reefs to the east support near pristine reefs with high coral cover and development (Maragos 1988).

--- SENTENCE 1836 ---
Only brief snorkeling observations were possible at Wake, but shallow ocean reefs displayed high coral cover while lagoon reefs showed very little coral cover, possibly the result of the lingering effects of WWII-era dredging, filling and causeway construction (J. Marragos, pers.

--- SENTENCE 1837 ---
comm.).

## 2.4 Invertebrates (Crustaceans, Molluscs, Echinoderms)

Important invertebrate resources in most countries belong to three major taxa: crustaceans (mostly crayfish), molluscs (especially clams and octopus) and echinoderms (especially sea cucumbers which are processed into "trepang" or "beche de mer", and urchins whose gonads are edible).

--- SENTENCE 1838 ---
All of these invertebrates are used as food.

--- SENTENCE 1839 ---
In addition, some molluscs have been used as money, decorative jewelry, medicine, building materials, tools, horns and objects of art (Uchida 1983), and sea cucumbers have been used as bait, poisons for stunning fish and for pig food (Preston 1993).

--- SENTENCE 1840 ---
The status of each of these resources is as follows:

## 2.4.1 American Samoa

The coral reefs of American Samoa support a rich molluscan fauna, which may include approximately 2,000 species (A. Kay pers.

--- SENTENCE 1841 ---
For example, Birkeland et al. (1987, 1994, 1996) recorded almost 200 species of marine gastropods on Tutuila Island alone.

--- SENTENCE 1842 ---
However, very little is known about the distribution and abundance of most species.

--- SENTENCE 1843 ---
One exception is giant clams.

--- SENTENCE 1844 ---
Giant clams (*Tridacna* spp.

--- SENTENCE 1845 ---
and *Hippopus hippopus*) have been heavily exploited throughout much of their range in the Pacific Islands (Green & Craig 1996), and there is a real danger of extinction facing some of the larger species (Adams & Dalzell in press).

--- SENTENCE 1846 ---
In the 1980s, IUCN listed the two largest species, *Tridacna gigas* and *T. derasa*, as threatened species and the international export of tridacnids is now regulated by the Convention on International Trade and Endangered Species (CITES).

--- SENTENCE 1847 ---
Little information exists on the status of clam stocks in most locations in the WPRFMC region.

--- SENTENCE 1848 ---
However, a recent study in the territorial waters of American Samoa has shown that clams (*T. maxima* and *T. squamosa*) are present only in very low densities in most of the archipelago, especially where human populations are high (Green & Craig 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1849 ---
One species, *Hippopus hippopus*, now appears to be locally extinct (Green & Craig 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1850 ---
In fact, the only place where a healthy population of giant clams still exists in Samoa is at Rose Atoll National Wildlife Refuge, where one species (*T. maxima*) is still very abundant (Green & Craig 1996)

--- SENTENCE 1851 ---
Thousands of species of crustaceans and echinoderms are also expected to occur in the Samoan Islands (L. Eldredge pers.

--- SENTENCE 1852 ---
Commercially important species know to occur include spiny lobsters (*Panulirus* spp.), slipper lobsters (*Scyllarides* spp.) and the xanthid crabs *Scylla* sp. and *Carpilius* sp. (USFWS 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1853 ---
At least 13 species of starfish are also known from American Samoa, including the crown-of-thorns starfish (Marsh 1974 in USFWS 1996, Birkeland et al. 1987, 1994, 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1854 ---
Very little information is known about the sponges of Samoa, with only a few species recorded to date (Kelly-Borge and Valentine 1995).

--- SENTENCE 1855 ---
Recent surveys provide some insight into the distribution and abundance of some of these species.

--- SENTENCE 1856 ---
For example, Hunter et al. (1993) described the abundance of some macro-invertebrates (those >1 cm in diameter, excluding cryptic and infaunal species) during their survey of the reefs on Ofu (see Corals and "Live Rock").

--- SENTENCE 1857 ---
They found that the most common macro-invertebrates in the southeastern lagoon at Ofu were sea cucumbers (up to 0.4 Stichopus/m²) and urchins (up to 0.04 Diadema/m²), while few edible molluscs (Tridacna or Trochus) were seen.

--- SENTENCE 1858 ---
They also noted that while local fishermen caught numerous octopus (about 10 per day), none were seen in the survey area.

--- SENTENCE 1859 ---
Low numbers of the crown-of-thorns starfish, Acanthaster planci, were also observed in the lagoon (maximum of 1 or 2 observed per site), and the urchin Diadema, the sea cucumber Bohadschia argus, and giant clams (Tridacna spp.) were also common at one site.

--- SENTENCE 1860 ---
Hunter et al. (1993) also surveyed three sites on the reef slope on Ofu (see *Corals and "Live Rock"*).

--- SENTENCE 1861 ---
They reported that urchins (*Echinothrix* sp.) were common at one site in front of the airport, while one *Tridacna* was recorded at the site in front of the Hurricane house, and one *Tridacna* and 8 juvenile *Trochus* were recorded at the other site in front of Ofu Village.

--- SENTENCE 1862 ---
Hunter

et al. (1993) also commented on the apparent absence or decreased abundance of two important sea cucumber species (*Thelenota ananas* and *Actinopyga mauritiana*), which Itano and Buckley (1988) reported were common on the reefs at Ofu.

--- SENTENCE 1863 ---
In another study, Birkeland et al. (1987, 1994, 1996) have described the macroinvertebrate fauna of Fagatele Bay National Marine Sanctuary (FBNMS) on Tutuila, based on two surveys over the last ten years: 1988 (Birkeland et al. 1994) and 1995 (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1864 ---
In 1985, echinoderms were found to be the dominant group of benthic invertebrates in FBNMS in terms of standing crop (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1865 ---
In 1995, echinoderms were still the dominant group of macroinvertebrates in the bay (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1866 ---
However, the pink-spined urchin *Echinometra mathaei* had decreased in abundance in most locations by an order of magnitude (and sometimes by >95%) from 1985 to 1995 (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1867 ---
This was considered of ecological importance to the bay, since *E. mathaei* is a major agent of bioerosion (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1868 ---
However, this reduction in population density of *E. mathaei* was seen as a healthy sign, since it was viewed as part of the natural recovery of the reefs after they were devastated by the crown-of-thorns starfish in 1979 (Birkeland et al. 1996, see *Corals and Live Rock*).

--- SENTENCE 1869 ---
In 1995, the small, burrowing echinoid *Echinostrephus aciculats* was the principal species, with densities ranging from 1 to 208 urchins per m<sup>2</sup> in sheltered and exposed areas respectively (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1870 ---
In contrast to *E. mathaei*, the densities of *E. aciculatus* have remained relatively unchanged over time (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1871 ---
Sponges were also dominant in sheltered locations in FBNMS in 1995 (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1872 ---
For example, the encrusting *Dysidea herbacea* species-complex formed mats as great as 4.4/m² in some places, covering considerable areas of substratum (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1873 ---
This sponge was not recorded in FBNMS in 1985, and its increase in abundance may be a successional stage in the natural recovery of the ecosystem (see above, Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1874 ---
Alcyonarians also comprise a conspicuous and abundant component of the macroinvertebrates fauna in FBNMS, with the number of genera recorded in the bay increasing from two to three from 1985 to 1996 (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1875 ---
One small species (Cladiella sp. cf.

--- SENTENCE 1876 ---
C. pachyclados: densities > 5 colonies/ m²), occurred in the highest frequency of all macroinvertebrates in the bay in 1995 (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1877 ---
Large soft coral species (e.g. Sinularia and Lobophytum) were present, but in relatively low densities (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1878 ---
Encrusting mats of the zooanthid Palythoa tuberculosa were also widespread in the sanctuary (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1879 ---
However, holothurians remain uncommon, with only two individuals of Actinopyga mauritiana recorded in the bay in 1995 (none were recorded in 1985:

--- SENTENCE 1880 ---
Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1881 ---
Gastropods were the most diverse group of macroinvertebrates recorded in FBNMS in both 1985 and 1995 (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1882 ---
Predatory neogastropods were the most diverse, accounting for 74% of the gastropod assemblage and 40% of the total macroinvertebrate diversity in the bay in 1995 (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1883 ---
There was also an indication that the diversity of gastropods had increased in the bay, with the number of neogastropods increasing from 15 in 1985 to 20 in 1995

(Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1884 ---
Only a few individuals of food species (giant clams and octopus) were observed (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1885 ---
Birkeland et al. (1996) also surveyed the macroinvertebrates at ten other sites around Tutuila in 1995.

--- SENTENCE 1886 ---
They recorded a total of 96 species on the island, 4 sponge species, 18 soft coral species, 46 mollusc species (43 gastropods, 2 bivalves and 1 cephalopod), 7 crustacean species, 14 echinoderm species (2 crinoids, 5 echinoids, 4 asteroids, and 3 holothurians), 4 ascidian species, and three species of marine worm (1 platyhelminth and 2 polychaetes: Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1887 ---
Most macroinvertebrate species recorded on Tutuila (81 species) were seen in FBNMS (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1888 ---
The results of several recent coral reef surveys have shown that the crown-of-thorns starfish is only present in low numbers in American Samoa at present.

--- SENTENCE 1889 ---
data) did not observe large numbers of A. planci during her survey of all of the islands in American Samoa, although occasional individuals and feeding scars were encountered on most islands (except Swains).

--- SENTENCE 1890 ---
Similarly, Maragos et al. (1994) and Hunter et al. (1993) only recorded low numbers of starfish in their surveys of Tutuila and the Manu'a Group in 1991-1992, while Birkeland et al. (1996) recorded none in their survey of Tutuila in 1995.

--- SENTENCE 1891 ---
However, Mundy (1996) reported that there was evidence of a large population of A. planci on the reef slope in front of Olosega Village in 1995.

--- SENTENCE 1892 ---
Similarly, moderately high densities of starfish were also observed on several reefs on 'Upolu in Western Samoa by Green (1996a).

--- SENTENCE 1893 ---
As such, pockets of low to moderately high-density aggregations of the starfish do occur in the archipelago.

--- SENTENCE 1894 ---
However in general, the starfish are much more abundant on the reefs of Western Samoa than in American Samoa, possibly because of the well-developed lagoonal systems in Western Samoa.

## 2.4.2 Marianas (Guam and CNMI)

Thousands of species of crustaceans and echinoderms are expected to occur on the coral reefs of Guam and CNMI, but accurate information on species diversity and abundance are not available (L. Eldredge pers.

--- SENTENCE 1898 ---
Although to date, these reefs are know to support at least 1,300 mollusc species, 140 echinoderm species, 56 species of anomuran crustaceans, 31 species of soft corals and sea fans, and 68 species of sponge (Kropp et al. 1981, Eldredge et al. 1981, Carlson & Hoff 1981, Anon. 1981, Kay 1995, Kelly-Borges & Valentine 1995, Myers 1997, see Birkeland 1997b).

--- SENTENCE 1899 ---
No endemic crustacean or echinoderms have been identified in the area.

--- SENTENCE 1900 ---
in Myers 1997) reported that >1,300 mollusc species have been recorded from the southern Marianas, including Guam (> 200 bivalves, >700 prosobranch gastropods, and > 400 opisthobranchs).

--- SENTENCE 1901 ---
Less is known of the molluscan fauna of CNMI, although some information is available for the northern islands e.g. Vermeij et al (1983) recorded at least 300

species of shelled mollusc in the northern islands (north of Farallon de Medinilla).

--- SENTENCE 1902 ---
Of these, 18 were unknown or rare in the southern Marianas (mostly intertidal species e.g. limpets: Vermeij et al. 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1903 ---
In contrast, at least 22 species that were common in the southern Marianas were absent in the northern Marianas (intertidal and reef flat species: Vermeij et al. 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1904 ---
More recently, Kurozumi & Asakura (1994) recorded a total of 520 species of marine mollusc in the northern islands (see below).

--- SENTENCE 1905 ---
Giant clams are present in both Guam and CNMI (*Tridacna maxima* and *T. squamosa*), and they are still harvested wherever they are found (Hensley & Sherwood 1993).

--- SENTENCE 1906 ---
comm.) also noted that clams were abundant on the shallow reef at Arakane Reef in the western chain of seamounts in federal waters.

#### Invertebrate Resources on Guam

Of the large number of mollusc species recorded in Guam, only a few are harvested for food (Myers 1997).

--- SENTENCE 1907 ---
Molluscs that are among the most important food species include 24 species of giant clams, smaller clams, mussels, marine gastropods (e.g. turban and top shells), chitons, octopus and squid (Amesbury et al. 1986 in USFWS 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1908 ---
Trochus niloticus (= the top shell) was introduced from Belau to Saipan in the late 1930s and to Guam about two decades later, and is now abundant on reef flats and subtidally to a depth of a t least 12m on both islands (see Vermeij et al. 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1909 ---
At present, this is the only mollusc species to be taken in large quantities for subsistence and commercial purposes on Guam (Myers 1997).

--- SENTENCE 1910 ---
Smith (1979) reported that T. niloticus density appears to vary with exposure and reef topography around the island, with a higher, albeit more variable, density recorded on the leeward side (0.05 to 2.13 per 20m²) than on the windward side of the island (<0.1 per 20m²: Smith 1979).

--- SENTENCE 1911 ---
Different studies have also reported that this species prefers a variety of habitat types ranging from exposed outer slopes to lagoonal habitats at depths of 0-22m (see Stojkovich & Smith 1978).

--- SENTENCE 1912 ---
On Guam, this species appears to be segregated by size groups among habitat zones (Smith 1979), with the larger individuals found seaward of the outer reef flat (Stojkovich & Smith 1978).

--- SENTENCE 1913 ---
Given that juveniles characteristically inhabit shallow water, it possible that this species may be present in low numbers on the shallowest portions of the banks in federal waters (Myers 1997).

--- SENTENCE 1914 ---
However, Vermeij et al. (1983) did not record this species in their survey of the northern islands in 1970s and 80s.

--- SENTENCE 1915 ---
The top shell is used for food and jewelry (mother-of-pearl), and overharvesting of this species lead to a general decline in its numbers on Guam prior to World War II (Stojkovich & Smith 1978).

--- SENTENCE 1916 ---
By the 1970s, the top shell was sufficiently dense again to warrant a limited commercial fishery for this species so long as it was strictly regulated (Stojkovich and Smith 1978, Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 1917 ---
Several edible species of bivalve occur on Guam (Hedlund 1977).

--- SENTENCE 1918 ---
Only one species of giant clam is relatively common on the island (*Tridacna maxima*), where it occurs most frequently on the reef font (Stojkovich & Smith 1978).

--- SENTENCE 1919 ---
Two other species, *Hippopus hippopus* and *T*.

squamosa, have been recorded as rare on Guam (Stojkovich & Smith 1978).

--- SENTENCE 1920 ---
A forth species, Tridacna derasa has been recently introduced from Palau, but it is unknown whether it is reproducing on the island or not (Myers 1997).

--- SENTENCE 1921 ---
Myers (1997) noted that it is possible that T. maxima and T. squamosa may occur in federal waters, although it unlikely that H. hippopus or T. derasa will occur there since they show a preference for shallow, protected habitats.

--- SENTENCE 1922 ---
Stojkovich and Smith (1978) also reported that populations of other large edible bivalves (excluding tridacnids), were present on Guam where they were associated with the mangroves in Sasa Bay (Saxostrea mordax, Gafrarium tumidum and G. pectinatum) and the seagrass beds in Cocos Lagoon (e.g. Quidnipagaus palatum and Ctena spp.).

--- SENTENCE 1923 ---
Other mollusc species commonly taken for food in the Marianas include octopus (Octopus cyanea and O. ornatus), a squid (Sepioteuthis lessoniana), and a cuttlefish (Sepia latimanus: Myers 1997).

--- SENTENCE 1924 ---
The distribution and abundance of these species on Guam is largely unknown.

--- SENTENCE 1925 ---
However, Myers (1997) suggested that all of these species could be expected to occur in federal waters, as well as in the nearshore waters where they are most commonly harvested.

--- SENTENCE 1926 ---
Thirty species of holothurian occur on the reef flats and slopes on Guam, eight of which can be harvested for trepang or beche-de-mer (*Thelenota ananas, Bohadschia marmorata, Actinopyga maritiana, A. echinites, H. nobilis, H. edulis, H. atra* and *Stichopus chloronotus*: Rowe & Doty 1977).

--- SENTENCE 1927 ---
Rowe and Doty (1977) found that in general, the distribution of commercially valuable species around the island in the 1970s was patchy.

--- SENTENCE 1928 ---
*H. atra* was the most numerous species, and it was most abundant at Uruno (density=22/m²).

--- SENTENCE 1929 ---
Myers (1997) noted that sand flats on some of the offshore banks may be expected to support exploitable populations of sea cucumbers, but this has not been confirmed.

--- SENTENCE 1930 ---
Stojkovich and Smith (1978) surveyed sea urchins that are harvested for their ripe gonads on Guam (*Diadema* and *Echinothrix*).

--- SENTENCE 1931 ---
They reported that these species tended to occur on the outer reef flat and reef margin, since they favor shallow reef areas with small tunnels/overhangs in areas of good water motion.

--- SENTENCE 1932 ---
Urchins of all sizes were found in the same habitats and there appeared to be no segregation by size.

--- SENTENCE 1933 ---
Urchins were found on most of the reefs of Guam, but significant populations seemed to be limited to a few leeward reefs (Stojkovich and Smith 1978).

--- SENTENCE 1934 ---
D. savignyi was found in low numbers at all sites, except on the Piti reef flat where it was dominant.

--- SENTENCE 1935 ---
E. diadema was more evenly distributed among the sites, with the highest populations found at Tumon, Piti and Agana Bays.

--- SENTENCE 1936 ---
Previous studies in other locations have determined that these urchins tend to produce ripe gonads at monthly intervals throughout the year, and that individuals of each species tend to have synchronous gametogenesis, although the timing of gametogenesis probably varies among genera (see Stojkovich & Smith 1978).

--- SENTENCE 1937 ---
Stojkovich and Smith (1978 in Uchida 1983) examined sea urchins in Guam periodically for gonadal development but did not find any ripe individuals.

--- SENTENCE 1938 ---
The status of sea urchin populations on the banks in federal waters is unknown.

--- SENTENCE 1939 ---
However, Myers (1997) suggested that the two species that are commonly harvested on Guam (*Tripneustes* 

gratilla and Echinometra mathaei) may be absent or occur in low densities in federal waters since their preferred habitats (shallow reef flats and lagoons) are not present.

--- SENTENCE 1940 ---
There is no comprehensive list of the crustaceans on Guam, but several hundred species probably occur there (Myers 1997).

--- SENTENCE 1941 ---
Crustacean species that are targeted by local fishermen include four species of spiny lobster (Panulirus longipes, P. ornatus, P. penicillatus, and P. versicolor), one homarid, one slipper lobster (Scyllarus squamosus), one or more large species of mantis shrimp (Lysiosquilla spp.), and several species of crab (Carpilius maculatus, Etisus dentatus, E. utilis, Calappa hepatica and C. calappa).

--- SENTENCE 1942 ---
Very little information is available on the distribution and abundance of these species on Guam.

--- SENTENCE 1943 ---
However, Myers (1997) has suggested that most of them may be expected to occur in federal waters, except two of the spiny lobsters (P. longipes and P. ornatus).

--- SENTENCE 1944 ---
A recent survey of the macroinvertebrates at Andersen Air Base Marine Resource Preserve provides a useful description of the macroinvertebrate communities on the reef flat on the north side of the island (Amesbury et al. 1995).

--- SENTENCE 1945 ---
A total of 35 species of macroinvertebrates were recorded in the Preserve, which is rather low because many of the cryptic or nocturnal species would have been missed.

--- SENTENCE 1946 ---
However, this total is still greater than the 35 species recorded in Tumon Bay during a similar survey (see Amesbury et al. 1995).

--- SENTENCE 1947 ---
Amesbury et al. (1995) reported that the near-shore zone of the Andersen Air Base Marine Resource Preserve was characterized by low species richness (overall mean number per transect = 5.3), and that macroinvertebrate abundance was extremely variable.

--- SENTENCE 1948 ---
In general, they found that the conspicuous macroinvertebrates in this zone tended to become less abundant as the reef flat narrowed from west (e.g.  $648/m^2$ ) to east (e.g.  $36/m^2$ ).

--- SENTENCE 1949 ---
By comparison, invertebrate abundance tended to be lower in the mid-reef zone, although species richness was slightly higher and more variable (overall mean number per transect = 6.0) than in the near-shore area.

--- SENTENCE 1950 ---
One species, *Holothuria atra*, comprised >90% of all the invertebrates counted in both the near-shore and mid-reef zones, with densities ranging from 2-480 per  $100m^2$ .

--- SENTENCE 1951 ---
In general, species richness was highest on the near-crest zone (overall mean number = 9.0), but density was low (from 19 and 38 per  $m^2$ ).

--- SENTENCE 1952 ---
In 1993, Amesbury et al. (1993) completed a re-survey of the reefs in Tumon Bay.

--- SENTENCE 1953 ---
They compared their results with those done in a previous survey in 1977, and concluded that the populations of macroinvertebrates in Tumon Bay have been relatively stable during the 14 years between surveys.

--- SENTENCE 1954 ---
Amesbury et al. (1993) suggested that these results indicated that there were no changes taking place along the shoreline in Tumon Bay that were harmful to the invertebrates.

--- SENTENCE 1955 ---
In fact, some species had actually increased in abundance since the 1970s (e.g. the holothurians Actinopyga echinites and Stichopus chloronotus; and the sea urchin Echinometra mathaei: Amesbury et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 1956 ---
The cause of the increase in abundance of these species is unclear, but could be related to human impacts (e.g. overfishing leading to an increase in urchin density) or natural processes (e.g. recruitment variability).

#### Invertebrate Resources in CNMI

The invertebrate fauna of CNMI is less well known than that on Guam.

--- SENTENCE 1957 ---
However, more than 520 species of marine mollusc (including 4 chitons, 456 gastropods and 68 bivalves) have been recorded in the Northern Marianas, 190 of which were first recorded in 1992 (Kurozumi & Asakura 1994).

--- SENTENCE 1958 ---
Kurozumi and Asakura (1994) reported that most of the species were widely distributed in the Indo-western Pacific, while others appear to be locally distinct morphs or species (e.g. Sanhaliotis spp.

--- SENTENCE 1959 ---
that are endemic to the Northern Marianas and southern Japan (e.g. Nipponacmea boninensis).

--- SENTENCE 1960 ---
A recent survey of the crustacean fauna of the northern islands also recorded a total of 119 species, including: 26 species (6 families) of macruran decapod (1 stenopodid, 24 carideans, and 1 palinuran: Hayashi et al. 1994); 28 species (7 families) of anomuran crustacean (1 Callianassidae, 6 Coenobitidae, 9 Diogenidae, 3 Paguridae, 1 Galatheidae, 7 Porcelllanidae and 1 Hippidae: Asakura et al. 1994b); 62 species (13 families) of brachyuran crab (Takeda et al. 1994); and 2 species of stomatopod (Hamano 1994).

--- SENTENCE 1961 ---
Brachyuran families recorded included: Dromiidae, Dynomenidae, Majidae, Parthenopidae, Atelecyclidae, Portunidae, Xanthidae, Menippidae, Pilumnidae, Trapeziidae, Ocypodidae, Grapsidae, and Gecarcinidae (Takeda et al. 1994 in Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 1962 ---
Most of the species recorded in the Northern Marianas have a wide distribution in the tropical Indo-West Pacific (Hayashi et al. 1994).

--- SENTENCE 1963 ---
Irimura et al. (1994) recently recorded 15 species (12 families) of echinoderm in the northern islands (excluding holothurians).

--- SENTENCE 1964 ---
This included two crinoid species (Lamprometra palmata palmata and Annametra minuta), three asteroids (Acanthaster planci, Linckia multifora and L. laevigata), four ophiuroids (Amphipholis squamata, Ophiactis savignyi, Ophiocoma dentata and Ophiostriatus sp.), and five echinoids (Eucidaris metularia, Echinothrix diadema, Diadema sp., Nudechinus sp. and Echinometra mathaei).

--- SENTENCE 1965 ---
Of these species, eight were found to be new records for the Mariana Islands (see Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 1966 ---
Some information is available on the distribution and abundance of a range of macroinvertebrate species in CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 1967 ---
In 1988, Chandran (1988) described the patterns of distribution and abundance of **holothurians** in Saipan Lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 1968 ---
He recorded a total of 12 species, four of which are edible (*Holothuria atra, Stichopus chloronotus, Bohadschia marmorata and Actinopyga echinatus*), although only the last three are potentially harvestable on a commercial basis (Tsuda and Bryan 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1969 ---
, One species, *H. atra*, is occasionally harvested on a subsistence level (Tsuda and Bryan 1996).

--- SENTENCE 1970 ---
Chandran (1988) reported that sea cucumbers occurred in three habitat types in the lagoon: nearshore seagrass beds, midlagoon sand flats and outer rocky reef margins.

--- SENTENCE 1971 ---
He also noted that each species showed distinct habitat preferences, with species diversity and abundance being inversely proportional to the distance from shore.

--- SENTENCE 1972 ---
Diversity and abundance were highest in the nearshore sea grass beds, and lowest in the midlagoon sand flats.

--- SENTENCE 1973 ---
*Holothuria atra* occurred in all three habitat zones, while *Bohadschia marmorata* was found predominantly in high energy rocky reef margin areas where wave action was strong.

--- SENTENCE 1974 ---
In contrast, *Stichopus chloronotus* was found in

nearshore grass beds and the rocky outer reef margin, and showed partial separation of habitats when present along with *H. atra*.

--- SENTENCE 1975 ---
One edible species, *H. atra*, was recorded in harvestable quantities (Table 41), and large quantities of juveniles were observed in nearshore *Halodule uninvervis* sea grass beds for the first time.

--- SENTENCE 1976 ---
Chandran (1988) estimated the population size of 11 holothurian species in Saipan lagoon (Table 41).

--- SENTENCE 1977 ---
However, these estimates should be viewed with caution since they were based on limited survey data and an estimated surface area of the lagoon of 51.8 km<sup>2</sup> vs an estimate surface area of ~35 km<sup>2</sup> by Amesbury et al 1979 (see Gourley 1997, see below).

--- SENTENCE 1978 ---
Tsuda and Bryan (1996) did a follow up to Chandran's survey in 1996.

--- SENTENCE 1979 ---
They recorded nine edible species in Saipan Lagoon, six of which had not been previously identified by Chandran (1988): Actinopyga maritiana, Holothuria (Microthele) nobilis, H. (M.) fuscogilva, H. (Metriatyla) scabra, H. (Halodeima) edulis, and Theloneta aranus.

--- SENTENCE 1980 ---
Tsuda and Bryan (1996) also estimated the population sizes of sea cucumbers in Saipan Lagoon, and noted that their estimates were considerably lower than those reported by Chandran (see Tables 41 & 42).

--- SENTENCE 1981 ---
For example, three species, *Actinopyga echinites, Holothuria atra*, and *Stichopus chloronotus* were about 17 to 20 times less abundant in 1996 than they were in 1988 (Tables 41 & 42).

--- SENTENCE 1982 ---
However, Tsuda and Bryan (1996) suggested that the differences in population size were probably more the result of differences between the two survey methods, than differences in the actual abundance of holothurians.

--- SENTENCE 1983 ---
To be specific, Tsuda and Bryan (1996) suggested that Chandran's (1988) calculations were grossly overestimated, because of the failure to factor in zero abundance values in those habitats where no individuals were observed.

--- SENTENCE 1984 ---
However, Tsuda and Bryan (1996) did acknowledged that their population estimates may have been "underestimates" for undisclosed reasons.

--- SENTENCE 1985 ---
Estimated population sizes for each of 11 holothurian species in Saipan Lagoon in 1988 (from Gourley 1997 after Chandran 1988).

--- SENTENCE 1988 ---
However, this population is considered small for this species.

--- SENTENCE 1989 ---
Tsuda and Bryan (1996) concluded that because of the low numbers of sea cucumbers in Saipan Lagoon, the population should be best harvested at a subsistence level only.

--- SENTENCE 1990 ---
Tsuda and Bryan (1996) also did limited counts of holothurians along the seaward reef margin and slope areas of the Lighthouse Marine Preserve outside of Saipan Lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 1991 ---
This area was surveyed to obtain an estimate of "naturally occurring" sea cucumber populations and species diversity in the habitat type, which was being commercially exploited at the time (see *Patterns of Utilization*).

--- SENTENCE 1992 ---
Unfortunately, only eight *Actinopyga mauritiana* were observed in the Preserve, and no comments or conclusions were made in the report.

--- SENTENCE 1993 ---
Recently, DFW completed a survey of the sea cucumbers on the outer reef slopes on southern and western sides of Saipan.

--- SENTENCE 1994 ---
This survey was aimed at assessing the numbers of sea cucumbers remaining after the 1995-1997 harvest (see *Patterns of Utilization*).

--- SENTENCE 1995 ---
They estimated that a total of approximately 11,000 sea cucumbers remained in these areas (primarily *Actinopyga mauritiana* and *Holothuria noblis*), and that a large percentage of the population (93.7%) had been harvested (DFW unpubl.

Several earlier studies have also described the distribution and abundance of holothurians on Saipan.

--- SENTENCE 2000 ---
For example, Dickinson (1977 in Uchida 1983) described the holothurian fauna in Tanapag Harbor, Saipan.

--- SENTENCE 2001 ---
He found *Holothuria atra* to be the most abundant, which is one of the least marketable of the commercially valuable species (Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2002 ---
Dickinson (1977 in Uchida 1983) also found another commercially valuable species (*Stichopus chloronotus*) at Tanapag Harbor, although this species was not as widespread as some of the others encountered.

--- SENTENCE 2003 ---
Randall et al. (1985) also surveyed the macroinvertebrates in Tanapag Lagoon, and they reported that holothurians were the most abundant group of echinoderms in the lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 2004 ---
They also noted that holothurians occurred mostly in sandy areas, although some species were located in sea grass beds.

--- SENTENCE 2005 ---
*Holothuria atra* was the most abundant species, attaining a maximum density of 39.5/dm<sup>2</sup> (Randall et al. 1985).

--- SENTENCE 2006 ---
In contrast, Randall et al. (1988) found that holothurians were not abundant on the reef front at Obyan-Naftan reef complex in southern Saipan.

--- SENTENCE 2007 ---
More recently, Smith (1991) provided an assessment of the macroinvertebrate fauna in Laulau Bay on Saipan, including holothurians.

--- SENTENCE 2008 ---
He described differences between the macroinvertebrate communities in different locations and at different times, which he attributed to differences in habitat structure, exposure, fresh water run-off and silt loads during the rainy season, as well as human activities (reef walking).

--- SENTENCE 2009 ---
Smith (1991) reported that two of the most abundant species on the reef flat were *Holothuria atra* (max. density of  $38.2 \pm 14.43$  per 20 m<sup>2</sup>) and *Holothuria leucospilota* (max. density of  $17.0 \pm 10.31$  per 20 m<sup>2</sup>).

--- SENTENCE 2010 ---
In contrast, one of the most abundant species in the spur and groove zone was *Stichopus chloronotus* (up to  $25.2 \pm 6.14$  per 20 m<sup>2</sup>).

--- SENTENCE 2011 ---
Limited information is also available on the holothurians on Rota.

--- SENTENCE 2012 ---
For example, Smith et al. (1989) described the holothurian fauna at Talakhaya on the southern coast.

--- SENTENCE 2013 ---
They found that the fauna varied among habitat zones.

--- SENTENCE 2014 ---
*Holothuria atra* was the most abundant species on the intertidal bench, although *H. leucospilota* and *Actinopyga mauritiana* were present also.

--- SENTENCE 2015 ---
Holothurians were also present in water-filled depressions on the emergent limestone ridge, but only in low numbers (*H. leucospilota* and *H. atra*: Smith et al. 1989).

--- SENTENCE 2016 ---
In contrast, sea cucumbers were dominant on the outer reef flat in terms of biomass, especially *Actinopyga mauritiana*, *H. atra* and *H. leucospilota* (Smith et al. 1989).

--- SENTENCE 2017 ---
Smith et al. (1989) also described the holothurian fauna at nearby Gagani, and found that the inner reef flat at this site supported a relatively dense population of *H. atra* and *Stichopus chloronotus*.

--- SENTENCE 2018 ---
Other species observed on Rota during this survey included *H. edulis* at Gagani, and *Heterocentrotus mammillatus* at Talakhaya (Smith et al. 1989).

--- SENTENCE 2019 ---
In a less intensive survey, Randall and Smith (1988) reported that *Actinopyga mauritiana* was most widespread species on the bench platform along the northeast coast of Rota.

--- SENTENCE 2020 ---
Other species observed in this area included *Holothuria atra*, *H. leucospilota*, and *H. difficilis* (Randall & Smith 1988).

--- SENTENCE 2021 ---
Several surveys have also commented on the distribution and abundance of **echinoid** species in CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 2022 ---
For example, Dickinson (1977 in Uchida 1983) noted that the most frequently observed urchin in Tanapag Harbor, Saipan was *Mespilia globulus*, which was most abundant in a narrow rubble zone (Dickinson 1977 in Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2023 ---
More recently, a survey by Randall et al (1985) found that urchins were the second most abundant group of echinoderms in Tanapag Lagoon (after holothurians), and that they were generally restricted to areas of hard substrate, so their density increased towards the reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 2024 ---
*Echinothrix diadema* and *Echinometra mathaei* were abundant on the reef margin, while *Diadema savignyi* and *D. setosum* were mostly encountered

in the outer moat area (Randall et al. 1985).

--- SENTENCE 2025 ---
Similar patterns of distribution and abundance of echinoderms were observed on the northern Tanapag reef platform by Randall et al. (1987).

--- SENTENCE 2026 ---
Randall et al. (1988) described the echinoderm assemblages on the Obyan-Naftan reef complex in southern Saipan (Randall et al. 1988).

--- SENTENCE 2027 ---
They reported that the reef flat assemblages were similar to those described at Tanapag Lagoon (see above).

--- SENTENCE 2028 ---
Randall et al. (1988) also described the echinoderm assemblages on the reef front, and found that there were characterized by a diverse assemblage where echinoids were more abundant than holothurians.

--- SENTENCE 2029 ---
The most abundant sea urchin was *Echinostrephus* cf.

--- SENTENCE 2030 ---
aciculatus, with smaller numbers of *Echinometra mathaei* and *Echinothrix diadema* present also.

--- SENTENCE 2031 ---
More recently, Smith (1991) described the macroinvertebrate fauna in Laulau Bay on Saipan (see above), including sea urchins.

--- SENTENCE 2032 ---
He found that *Echinometra aciculatus* was one of the most abundant species in the spur and groove zone (up to  $89.9 \pm 27.1$  per  $20 \text{ m}^2$ ).

--- SENTENCE 2033 ---
*Echinometra mathaei* was also abundant in the spur and grove zone, and both *E. mathaei* and *Echinostrephus aciculatus* were abundant on the submarine terrace (up to  $10.0 \pm 5.34$  per  $20 \text{ m}^2$  for *E. mathaei* and  $37.6 \pm 13.4$  per  $20 \text{ m}^2$  for *E. aciculatus*).

--- SENTENCE 2034 ---
Limited information is also available on the sea urchins on Rota.

--- SENTENCE 2035 ---
For example, Smith et al. (1989) noted that echinoderms were the dominant element of the macroinvertebrate community on the reef slope at Talakhaya and Gagani on the southern side of the island.

--- SENTENCE 2036 ---
The most abundant species were the boring echinoids *

--- SENTENCE 2037 ---
Echinostrephus aciculatus* and *Echinometra mathaei* (Smith et al. 1989).

--- SENTENCE 2038 ---
Less abundant species in the area included *Echinothrix diadema* (Smith et al. 1989).

--- SENTENCE 2039 ---
Similarly, Randall and Smith (1988) reported that *Echinothrix diadema* was present in the channels on the bench platform along the northeast coast.

--- SENTENCE 2040 ---
Some information is available on the distribution and abundance of **mollusc** species in CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 2041 ---
One of the most commercially valuable molluscs is the gastropod *Trochus niloticus* (Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2042 ---
The shell of this species is used for the manufacture of buttons for the fashion industry, and the meat is used by local Pacific Island and Asian communities for subsistence use (Adams et al. 1994 in Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2043 ---
This species was introduced to CNMI in 1938 when the Japan South Seas Government brought 2,974 live trochus from Palau and released them in Saipan waters (Adams et al. 1994).

--- SENTENCE 2044 ---
From this successful introduction, the reefs of Guam, Tinian, Rota and Agrihan were later seeded.

--- SENTENCE 2045 ---
This resource is limited to the shallow fringing and barrier reef systems of nearshore waters in CNMI (see above).

--- SENTENCE 2046 ---
DFW established a moratorium on trochus harvest in CNMI in 1982 (Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2047 ---
In order to determine if the resources were sufficient to withstand a temporary lifting of the moratorium, DFW (with the assistance of SPC) conducted a trochus assessment survey of Saipan, Tinian and Rota in 1992 (Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2048 ---
Based on the results of this survey, potential harvest estimates were developed for each of the three islands (Table 43).

--- SENTENCE 2049 ---
However, these estimates should be used with caution (Adams et al. 1994 in Gourley).

--- SENTENCE 2050 ---
Based on the survey data, CNMI trochus densities were considered to be "less than half of what would normally be considered to be an optimally exploited fishery in some other countries" (see Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2051 ---
Although density values are low for exploitable-size trochus, recruitment fishing is not believed to be a problem at present because of the "high densities" of juvenile shells observed at several areas along the Saipan barrier reef flat (Adams et al. 1994 in Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2052 ---
Potential trochus harvest estimated for Saipan, Tinian and Rota (from Gourley 1997 after Adams et al. 1994).

Several surveys have described the distribution and abundance of other mollusc species in CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 2054 ---
Dickinson (1977 in Uchida 1983) surveyed molluscs in Tanapag Harbor, Saipan, and reported that the most frequently encountered gastropod species were *Lambis lambis* and *Cypraea erosa*, and the most abundant bivalve was *Saxostrea morda* (see Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2055 ---
Dickinson's list of major invertebrate species from Tanapag Harbor also included several species of shells that are of commercial value either for consumption or to collectors (Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2056 ---
Randall et al. (1985) also described the distribution and abundance of molluscs in Tanapag Lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 2057 ---
They reported that gastropods were the most common class of molluscs in the area.

--- SENTENCE 2058 ---
Some gastropods (cerithids and buccinids) were present in the shallows where they were "too numerous to count" (estimated density 200 per m²).

--- SENTENCE 2059 ---
Similarly vermetid molluscs were also present in numbers "too numerous to count" in some situations (outer reef moat and reef margin: estimated density 100-150 per m²).

--- SENTENCE 2060 ---
Randall et al. (1985) also noted that *Trochus niloticus* and *Cyprae moneta* were common in the outer reef moat and reef margin areas.

--- SENTENCE 2061 ---
In contrast, bivalves were predominantly encountered "scattered" in sandy areas between the shallows and the midmoat region.

--- SENTENCE 2062 ---
One exception were the tridacnid clams, which were common from the middle of the moat to the inner reef margin, because of their need to anchor on hard substrates.

--- SENTENCE 2063 ---
Similar patterns of distribution and abundance of molluscs were observed on the northern Tanapag reef platform by Randall et al. (1987).

--- SENTENCE 2064 ---
A similar survey by Randall et al. (1988) reported that predatory molluscs (Orders Mesogastropoda and Neogastropoda) were the most diverse group of molluscs on the reef flat at Obyan-Naftan (southern Saipan), with the greatest diversity exhibited by the family Conidae.

--- SENTENCE 2065 ---
However, the most abundant gastropod on the reef flat was the introduced species *Trochus niloticus*.

--- SENTENCE 2066 ---
Randall et al. (1988) also reported that epibenthic molluscs were slightly less diverse

on the reef front than on the reef flat, and that reasonable numbers of giant clams (*Tridacna maxima*) were present on the reef front.

--- SENTENCE 2067 ---
A total of 85 species of macroinvertebrates were observed on the Obyan-Naftan reef during the survey.

--- SENTENCE 2068 ---
More recently, Smith (1991) provided an assessment of the macroinvertebrate fauna in Laulau Bay on Saipan.

--- SENTENCE 2069 ---
He noted that giant clams were uncommon in the spur and groove zone at this site  $(2.2 \pm 1.92 \text{ per } 20 \text{ m}^2)$ .

--- SENTENCE 2070 ---
He also noted that echinoderms were the most abundant group in Laulau Bay, which conflicted with the results of an earlier study that found that gastropods were the most commonly collected macroinvertebrates encounted in the area (88 species: PBEC 1984).

--- SENTENCE 2071 ---
Limited information is also available on the molluscs on Rota.

--- SENTENCE 2072 ---
For example, Randall and Smith (1988) reported that molluscs were the most diverse taxon of benthic invertebrates on the bench platform along the northeast coast.

--- SENTENCE 2073 ---
Abundant species included periwinkles, nerites and limpets in the supratidal community, muricid snails in the littoral zone, and vermetid snails in the subtidal zone (Randall & Smith 1988).

--- SENTENCE 2074 ---
No molluscs important in the coral reef fishery in CNMI were observed on this reef (Randall & Smith 1988).

--- SENTENCE 2075 ---
Smith et al. (1989) also described the molluscan fauna on the reefs on the southeast coast of Rota at Talakhaya.

--- SENTENCE 2076 ---
They noted that molluscs were the dominant group of macroinvertebrates in all reef zones, except on the reef front.

--- SENTENCE 2077 ---
Dominant groups in each zone included: nerites, periwinkles, and the bubble shell *Haminoea cymbalum* in the intertidal zone; muricids, conids, vermetids, and limpets on the emergent limestone ridge; muricids, vasids, mitrids, conids, and bubble shells on the outer reef platform, and muricids and conids on the reef slope (Smith et al. 1989).

--- SENTENCE 2078 ---
Other molluscs observed on the reef slope included several species targeted in the local fishery, such as octopus (*Octopus cyanea*) and the giant clam *Tridacna maxima* (Smith et al. 1989).

--- SENTENCE 2079 ---
In particular, giant clams were observed on every transect, and ranged in size from about 5-25 cm in valve diameter (Smith et al. 1989).

--- SENTENCE 2080 ---
Smith et al. (1989) also described the molluscan fauna on the reef at nearby Gagani, and found the fauna to be similar, although less diverse, than at Talakhaya.

--- SENTENCE 2081 ---
Smith et al. (1989) and Randall and Smith (1988) both commented on the absence of the topshell *Trochus niloticus* at their study sites on Rota.

--- SENTENCE 2082 ---
They noted that while this species was known to occur on the island, it did not appear to be well established.

--- SENTENCE 2083 ---
Spiny lobsters are the primary **crustacean** resource in CNMI, and lobsters are always in demand in the local restaurants on Saipan (Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2084 ---
Three species of spiny lobster have been captured in the Northern Marianas: *Panulirus femoristriga*, *P. penicillatus* and *P. versicolor* (Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2085 ---
To date, only two trapping studies have provided some insight into their distribution and abundance in CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 2086 ---
The first study was done around Guam and CNMI in the 1970s, and found that spiny lobsters were caught at a rate of 2.7-3.6kg per trap in depths of 13-15m at Rota, which is believed to have the highest concentration of spiny lobsters in the

Commonwealth (Harrington 1977 in Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2087 ---
By comparison, no lobsters were caught at Tinian (Harrington 1977 in Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2088 ---
The second trapping study was done at 22 stations in the Mariana Islands (including Guam) in 1978, and captured only six spiny lobsters: five in CNMI (three *P. penicillatus* off Alamagan Island and Farallon de Medinilla; and two *P femoristriga* off Saipan) and one in Guam (one *P. versicolor* at Galvez Bank: see Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2089 ---
This study concluded that either spiny lobsters do not occur in any abundance in waters 13 m or deeper in the Northern Marianas, or they do not enter baited traps in any appreciable numbers (Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2090 ---
Uchida (1983) also suggested that the primary limiting factor in the population of spiny lobsters in CNMI might be the lack of suitable grounds on the volcanic islands, which have narrow reefs with little or no shelf zone.

--- SENTENCE 2091 ---
Unfortunately, no more recent surveys of the spiny lobster populations in CNMI have been done (Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2092 ---
However, Gourley (1997) reported that local fishermen say that there are few lobsters remaining on Saipan, and most of the spiny lobsters taken in the recent "Nearshore reef fish commercial survey" (see DFW 1994b) appear to have come from Tinian.

--- SENTENCE 2093 ---
Some limited information is also available on the distribution and abundance of other crustaceans in CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 2094 ---
For example, Smith (1991) provided an assessment of the macroinvertebrate fauna in Laulau Bay on Saipan (see above), including crustaceans.

--- SENTENCE 2095 ---
He noted that the hermit crab, Dardanus sp., was one of the most abundant species on both the reef flat (max. density of  $19.2 \pm 19.81$  per  $20 \text{ m}^2$ ) and in the spur and groove zone  $(38.6 \pm 22.2 \text{ per } 20 \text{ m}^2)$  in the bay.

--- SENTENCE 2096 ---
Dickinson (1977 in Uchida 1983) also noted that the gall crab, Hapalocarcinus marsupialis was very common in Tanapag Lagoon (Dickinson 1977 in Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2097 ---
Limited information is also available on the crustaceans on Rota.

--- SENTENCE 2098 ---
For example, Randall and Smith (1988) reported that the grapsid crab *Grapsus tenuicrustatus* was the most common and widespread species on the bench platform along the northeast coast.

--- SENTENCE 2099 ---
Other abundant crustaceans in the area included coenobitid and calcinid hermit crabs, ghost crabs and burrowing shrimp.

--- SENTENCE 2100 ---
No crustaceans of commercial importance were observed in this survey, although spiny lobsters and edible crabs (*Carpilius maculatus* and *Etisus* sp.) are reputed to be abundant on the reef margin in the area (Randall & Smith 1988).

--- SENTENCE 2101 ---
Very little is known about the distribution and abundance of **other macroinvertebrates** in CNMI, although some information is available for Saipan.

--- SENTENCE 2102 ---
For example, Randall et al. (1988) reported that soft corals were abundant on the reef slope (mostly *Sinularia* and some *Lobophytum*) at Obyan-Naftan, and

--- SENTENCE 2103 ---
Randall et al. (1985) noted that ascidians and sipunculid worms were abundant in Tanapag Lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 2104 ---
Some studies have also noted the presence of other invertebrates on Rota.

--- SENTENCE 2105 ---
For example, Randall and Smith (1988) reported that formaniferans, sponges and polychaete worms were abundant on the bench platform along the northeast side of Rota.

--- SENTENCE 2106 ---
Similarly, Smith et al. (1989) noted that

several other macroinvertebrates were present on the reefs on the southeast side of Rota, including encrusting sponges (including *Dysidea* sp.) and soft corals (*Sinularia* sp.).

--- SENTENCE 2107 ---
To date, the majority of information available on the distribution and abundance of macroinvertebrates in CNMI is for the southern islands (primarily Saipan: see above).

--- SENTENCE 2108 ---
In contrast, very little known of the macroinvertebrate resources of the **northern islands**, although some information is available.

--- SENTENCE 2109 ---
For example, Eldredge et al (1977) reported that the fauna of Maug Lagoon was typical for the Indo-Pacific, and comprised a total of 130 species of non-sclearactinian macroinvertebrates, including 64 gastropod species (18 families including at least 24 opisthobranch species), and 21 species of echinoderm.

--- SENTENCE 2110 ---
Eldredge et al. (1977a) also noted that three gastropod species (two *Haliotis* spp. and *Purpura persica*) were present on Maug, which have not been recorded in the southern Marianas (primarily Guam).

--- SENTENCE 2111 ---
Similarly, the land hermit crab *Coenobita perlata* was common on the shore at Maug, but is rare on Guam (Eldredge et al. 1977a).

--- SENTENCE 2112 ---
Eldredge et al. (1977a) also reported that the short-spined sea urchin *Colobocentrotus mertensi* was common on intertidal boulders on Maug, with densities recorded as high as 20-26 per 0.25 m².

--- SENTENCE 2113 ---
Other macroinvertebrates recorded at Maug include four soft coral species and a black coral (*Cirripathes* sp.: Eldredge 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2114 ---
Virtually no information is available on the invertebrates on the other northern islands, although Eldredge (1983) reported that the sea urchin *Diadema setosum* and the asteroid *Linckia multifora* were abundant on Agrihan.

--- SENTENCE 2115 ---
Eldredge (1983) also recorded a few species of intertidal organism on Uracas, including gastropods (*Littorina pintado* and *Cellana* sp.), crabs (*Grapsus tenuicrustatus*) and sea urchins (*Colobocentrotus mertensi*), which he believed were representative of the first stages of recolonization of the newly deposited shoreline.

--- SENTENCE 2116 ---
The abundant invertebrates in the intertidal zone have also been recorded at Anatahan and Asuncion.

--- SENTENCE 2117 ---
They include gastropods (*Littorina pintado, Nerita plicata* and *Purpura persica*) at Anatahan, and abalone (*Haliotis* sp.) and the sea urchin *C. mertensi* at Ascuncion (Eldredge 1983).

## 2.4.3 Hawaii

Hawaii's coral reefs support diverse communities of invertebrates, which vary as a function of depth, exposure and three-dimensional relief of their habitats (Fielding & Robinson 1987 in Smith 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2118 ---
Hawaii's marine invertebrate fauna comprises many species, including at least 884 crustacean species (Eldredge 1995), 1,071 mollusc species (Kay 1995), 278 echinoderm species (see Eldredge & Miller 1995), and 98 species of sponge (Kelly-Borges & Valentine 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2119 ---
Endemism is estimated to be about 20% for molluscs (Fielding & Robinson 1987 in USFWS 1996, Eldredge & Miller 1995), and ~3%, 30% and 54% for crustaceans, sponges and echinoderms respectively (see Eldredge & Miller 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2120 ---
Economically important invertebrates include lobsters, crabs, octopus and limpet (Smith 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2121 ---
Giant clams are naturally absent from the Hawaiian Islands (USFWS 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2122 ---
The distribution and abundance of macroinvertebrates in Hawaii have been described by several surveys.

--- SENTENCE 2123 ---
For example, Okamoto and Kawamoto (1980 in Friedlander 1996) recorded 63 species of macroinvertebrates in their five-year study of the NWHI (mostly molluscs, echinoderms and

crustaceans).

--- SENTENCE 2124 ---
They found that the most common macroinvertebrates observed in the lava rock and limestone habitats included the sea urchin (*Colobocentrotus atratus*), two molluscs (pipipi and periwinkles: Families Neritidae and Littorinidae respectively), and the a'ama or rock crab (*Grapsus grapsus*).

--- SENTENCE 2125 ---
Okamoto and Kawamoto (1980 in Friedlander 1996) also noted that economically and culturally important limpet (opihi) was present in the splash zone at La Perouse Pinnacle and Nihoa Island in densities of 1/m² and ~50/m² respectively.

--- SENTENCE 2126 ---
(1985 in Friedlander 1996) also described the benthic invertebrate community on a number of reefs in the NWHI based on collections from dead reef substrate (Table 44).

--- SENTENCE 2127 ---
They found crustaceans to be the dominant group of benthic organisms (mostly small crabs and shrimp), followed by polychaetes and molluscs (mostly gastropods: Table 44).

--- SENTENCE 2128 ---
By comparison, Sorden (1984 in Friedlander 1996) sampled the benthic invertebrates in the sand habitat at the lagoon at Midway Atoll, and found the most abundant organisms to be polychaete worms and molluscs.

--- SENTENCE 2129 ---
Other invertebrates recorded in the samples included isopods, tanaids, gammarids and sipunculids (see Friedlander 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2130 ---
It is also known that the Hawaiian black-lip pearl oyster (*Pinctada margaritifera galtsoffi*) was once common at Midway, but it has become increasingly rare ever since western contact in the Hawaiian Islands (USFWS Biological Summary of Midway Atoll).

--- SENTENCE 2131 ---
However, there has been a recent attempt to re-establish the pearl oyster at Midway (USFWS Biological Summary of Midway Atoll).

--- SENTENCE 2132 ---
Recently, Polovina et al. (1996) reported that there was a decline in recruitment of the spiny lobster *Panulirus marginatus* from the 1980s to 1990s, which was thought be the result of a decline in productivity rather than the result of overfishing (Polovina and Mitchum 1992 in Polovina et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2133 ---
At present, these lobsters are currently managed by WPRFMC via a Crustacean FMP, and will not be considered in detail in this report.

--- SENTENCE 2134 ---
However as Friedlander (1996) noted, this species is an important link in the trophic food web in the nearshore coral reef ecosystems of the NWHI.

## 2.4.4 Other U.S. Pacific Islands

No detailed surveys have been completed on the invertebrate communities on most of the Other U.S. Pacific Islands, although some information does exist for Johnston Atoll.

--- SENTENCE 2135 ---
For example Amerson & Shelton (1976) recorded 58 species of molluscs and 75 species of crustaceans at Johnston, although this is considered to be an underestimate (Cooke 1986).

--- SENTENCE 2136 ---
More recently, a survey of the non-sessile invertebrates at Johnston showed that the most abundant species were echinoderms, including holothurians (*Holothuria atra*), echinoids (*Echinometra oblonga, E. mathaei, Diadema paucispinua, Heterocentrotus mammillatus* and *Tripneustes gratilla*) and asteroids (*Linckia* sp.:

--- SENTENCE 2137 ---
Irons et al. 1984).

--- SENTENCE 2138 ---
Other less abundant species recorded at Johnston included the echinoids *E. calamaris/diadema*, the corallivorous starfish

Acanthaster planci, unidentified ophuroids, some molluscs (Cypraea tigris and unidentified bivalves), sponges and zooanthids (Irons et al. 1984).

In contrast, virtually no information is available on the invertebrate communities on the other U.S. possessions.

Although, giant clams (*Tridacna maxima*) are known to be abundant in the waters surrounding Howland and Baker Islands (USFWS 1996) and they have been recorded from Jarvis Island also (USFWS 1986).

#### 2.5 Algae

Algae or "seaweed" is harvested for a variety of reasons.

--- SENTENCE 2159 ---
In many countries, seaweeds are important as a food resource for humans or livestock, as well as a source of extracted chemicals used as food additives or in the production of cosmetics or pharmaceuticals (Hunt et al. 1982, Moss & Doty 1987, South 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2160 ---
The seaweed industry includes harvesting naturally occurring populations as well as species cultured via aquaculture, and the worldwide wholesale value of this industry exceeds \$2 billion annually (Moss & Doty 1987, Glenn & Pfund 1992).

--- SENTENCE 2161 ---
The majority of commercially important seaweeds (95%) originate in Asia and the Pacific, 79% of which are cultured (Glenn & Pfund 1992)

--- SENTENCE 2162 ---
The seaweeds of the tropical Pacific Islands are not well understood, and their potential as a resource has scarcely been developed (South 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2163 ---
However, their value may be considerable.

--- SENTENCE 2164 ---
Throughout the region, human consumption of seaweeds is widespread, although few detailed statistics are available on the quantities harvested (South 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2165 ---
In addition to harvesting "wild stocks", there is also considerable potential for the cultivation of seaweeds in the region.

--- SENTENCE 2166 ---
One potential problem for the seaweed industry is the seasonal variation in toxicity of some species (e.g. *Gracilaria tsudai*), which has already lead to at least one death in Guam (Biggs et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2167 ---
The following is a synopsis of the limited information available on the algal resources in the U.S. Pacific Islands:

## 2.5.1 American Samoa

To date, approximately 200 species of algae have been recorded from American Samoa, although it is expected that up to 400 species may occur there (I. Abbott pers.

--- SENTENCE 2168 ---
Two species of seagrasses are also know from the Samoan Islands, *Halophila ovalis* and *Syringodium isoetifolium* (Coles & Kuo 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2169 ---
A couple of recent surveys provide some insight into the distribution and abundance of algae on the reefs of Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 2170 ---
For example, Hunter et al. (1993) described the macroalgal assemblages on the reefs in the National Park on Ofu.

--- SENTENCE 2171 ---
They found that algal cover was relatively low at all sites surveyed (6.2 to 17.3 % cover), and that the dominant species were red coralline algae and small

turf forming species of red, brown and green algae.

--- SENTENCE 2172 ---
Larger growth forms were primarily limited to vertical surfaces in the lagoon, and to specific areas of the reef crest, such as adjacent to deep channels.

--- SENTENCE 2173 ---
Hunter et al. (1993) also described the structure and zonation of coral and algal communities at Ofu.

--- SENTENCE 2174 ---
They noted that "the basic structure of the reef at Ofu was very typical of tropical Pacific reefs, with the outer reef slope dominated by corals up to a depth of about 10-15 ft.

--- SENTENCE 2175 ---
From 10 to 15 ft up to and including the reef crest, coralline algae and small turf forming algae were dominant.

--- SENTENCE 2176 ---
The reef lagoon area was again dominated by corals, with larger fleshy algae confined mostly to the lower vertical sides of the reef structure and small caves, and small turf algae confined to the lower non-living parts of erect corals and rubble areas.

--- SENTENCE 2177 ---
The immediate shoreline was mostly sand, although there were a few areas with basalt boulders or hard sandstone with small filamentous algae growing on them."

--- SENTENCE 2178 ---
Hunter et al. (1993) concluded that these coral and algal communities were indicative of a low nutrient pristine tropical reef with extensive grazing by fish and invertebrates.

--- SENTENCE 2179 ---
In another study, Birkeland et al. (1987, 1994, 1996) described the algal communities in Fagatele Bay National Marine Sanctuary (FBNMS) on Tutuila, based on two surveys over the last ten years: 1988 (Birkeland et al. 1994) and 1995 (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2180 ---
In the latest survey (1995), a total of 26 species were recorded in the sanctuary (Birkeland et al. 1996) with an overall cover of 75% (s=12), most of which was crustose and articulate coralline algae (69%, s=15: Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2181 ---
One very common component of the coralline algae, *Peysonnelia* (25% cover), had formed a formed a reddish crust over dead corals and rubble over large areas, especially at 10-12 m depth (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2182 ---
Another coralline, *Porolithon onkodes*, was the most conspicuous component of the algal cover throughout the sanctuary (up to 80% cover), and appeared to have formed an almost continuous smooth crust covering in the bay, cementing and stabilizing the loose surface below (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2183 ---
In 1995, this *Porolithon* crust showed relatively little evidence of epiphytic algal growth, with only *Gelidium pussilum*, *Ceramium* and *Herposiphonia* found adhered to the crust's surface (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2184 ---
*Amphiroa* and *Chilosporum*, other common components of the coralline algal assemblage, were also frequently found entangled with other algal species forming dense clumps (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2185 ---
The algal composition of these clumps was similar to that of algal turfs and was composed of species such as *Dictyota*, *Dictyopteris*, *Ceramium*, *Polysiponia*, *Jania*, *Herposiphonia*, *Gelidium*, *Gelidiopsis*, *Gelidiella*, *Sphacelaria*, and *Pterocladia* (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2186 ---
Comparisons of the algal assemblages in the two surveys were difficult to make, because the surveys were conducted at different times of the year, and many of the species are seasonal (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2187 ---
However, comparisons of the existing data suggest that encrusting and articulate coralline algal cover has increased, while the cover of non-coralline species has decreased (Birkeland et al. 1996, Table 45).

--- SENTENCE 2188 ---
Birkeland et al. (1996) suggested that the prevalence of coralline algae, especially *Porolithon onkodes*, on the reefs in FBNMS has played an important role in the recovery of these reefs from two recent hurricanes (see *Corals and "Live Rock"*).

--- SENTENCE 2189 ---
The coralline algae appears to have assisted in coral reef recovery by stabilizing the reef by growing over and cementing dead corals, and by providing a suitable substratum for coral recruitment (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2190 ---
Given the critical role of coralline algae in reef recovery in FBNMS, it is important to note that two coralline algal "diseases" were observed on the reefs in the bay: CLOD or "coralline lethal orange disease" and a black "lichen-like" disease (Birkeland et al. 1996).

Birkeland et al. (1987, 1996) also surveyed the algal communities at ten other sites around Tutuila.

--- SENTENCE 2200 ---
They found that the algal assemblages at the other sites were similar to those described in Fagatele Bay (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2201 ---
They also found that the total number of plant species recorded in the survey was lower in 1995 (27 species) than it was in 1985 (53 species:

--- SENTENCE 2202 ---
Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2203 ---
However, the mean percent cover was slightly higher in the later survey (mean=56.1, s=24 in 1985; and mean=62.0, s=24 in 1995: Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2204 ---
Birkeland et al. (1996) also noticed that species of fleshy and filamentous algae that were recorded in 1985, seemed confined to algal turf assemblages or hidden in depressions and interstices in 1995, so many areas seemed to have a much "cleaner" appearance (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2205 ---
In contrast, coralline algae (especially encrusting coralline), showed an overall increase in percent cover from 38.2% (s=24) in 1985 to 48.1% (s=19) in 1995 (Birkeland et al. 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2206 ---
This high cover of pink coralline algae is presumed to be an important step in coral reef recovery after the recent hurricanes on Tutuila (see above).

--- SENTENCE 2207 ---
Macroalgae were also surveyed during the American Samoa Coral Resources Inventory in 1991-92.
