## 2.5.2 Marianas (Guam and CNMI)

Approximately 220 species of marine benthic algae are known from Guam and CNMI, as well as five species of seagrass (Tsuda 1981, Coles & Kuo 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2210 ---
These include: Cyanophyta (13 spp.), Chlorophyta (69 spp.), Phaeophyta (27 spp.) and Rhodophyta (111 spp.:

--- SENTENCE 2211 ---
Only four species of algae are commonly harvested for human consumption (Myers 1997): two greens (Caulerpa racemosa and Codium sp.), and two reds (Gracilaria edulis or G. tsudai, and Asparagopsis spp.).

--- SENTENCE 2212 ---
One species, Gracilaria tsudai, is frequently harvested commercially on Guam (Myers 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2213 ---
Little is known of the current patterns of distribution and abundance of commercial species on Guam or CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 2214 ---
Tsuda and co-workers produced numerous papers and reports on the patterns of distribution and abundance of marine algae in the Marianas in the 1970s (see Contributions of the University of Guam Marine Laboratory).

--- SENTENCE 2215 ---
However, this information is of little value for the current assessment since the data is 20-30 years old, and the algal communities are known to have changed dramatically since then (i.e. local sources report that algal cover has increased dramatically on Guam in recent decades: C. Birkeland and B. Richmond pers.

--- SENTENCE 2216 ---
com.).

## Algal Resources on Guam

There have been a few quantitative surveys of the algae on Guam in recent years, although these databases have only been summarized to a preliminary level at this time.

--- SENTENCE 2217 ---
One example, is the recent baseline survey of Andersen Air Force Base Marine Resource Preserve.

--- SENTENCE 2218 ---
Amesbury et al. (1995) recorded 73 species within the reserve, which is  $\sim^{1}/_{3}$  of the number recorded from Guam and about 50% more than the number recorded from Tumon Bay (55: see Amesbury et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2219 ---
Marine plant abundance, cover and species composition were quite variable because of seasonal variability, variation in herbivore abundance, and the impact of occasional strong wave action bought about by storms (Amesbury et al. 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2220 ---
As a result, algal cover was extremely patchy, ranging from 0-100% within a transect.

--- SENTENCE 2221 ---
Amesbury et al. 1993 also provided a comparison of the marine plants in Tumon Bay in 1977 and 1991.

--- SENTENCE 2222 ---
They reported that species diversity was similar in both surveys, although species composition had changed substantially (Amesbury et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2223 ---
Dominant species in 1977 included two blue-green algae species (*Microcoleus lyngbyaceus and Schizothrix calcicola*), two green algae (*Enteromorpha clathrata* and *Halimeda opuntia*) and two species of brown algae (*Padina borvana* and *Turbinaria ornata*).

--- SENTENCE 2224 ---
Only two of these species (*S. calcicola* and *P. borvana*) were considered dominant in 1991 also, along with six other species (*Boodlea composita, Jania capillacea, Polysiphonia* spp., *Cladophoropsis sundanensis, Gelidiella acerosa* and *Laurencia* sp.).

--- SENTENCE 2225 ---
Amesbury et al. (1993) also described patterns of zonation in the algal communities in the bay.

--- SENTENCE 2226 ---
*E. clathrata* was clearly the dominant algae in the sandy area along the shore (cover 11-48%: Amesbury et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2227 ---
However, it was not possible to determine if the standing crop of *Enteromorpha* had increased or decreased since 1977 (Amesbury et al. 1993), because this species has always been abundant in the area.

--- SENTENCE 2228 ---
Dominant algae from the shoreline to the outer reef edge included *Enteromorpha, Padina, Boodlea* and *Gelidiella* (Amesbury et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2229 ---
Davis (1982) surveyed the algal and seagrass communities in Cocos Lagoon, Guam in 1982.

--- SENTENCE 2230 ---
He recorded 97 species of marine plants in his survey, and showed that the rich algal communities were most diverse on the barrier reef and patch reef habitats (58 and 62 species recorded respectively) and least diverse on the lagoon floor and channel bottom (23 and 24 species respectively).

--- SENTENCE 2231 ---
Davis (1982) also compared the results of his survey with those of a previous survey of the area by Tsuda in 1975 (in Randall et al. 1975).

--- SENTENCE 2232 ---
He found that while the species in about half of the habitat types were similar in both surveys, the species in the other habitats were not.

--- SENTENCE 2233 ---
It was unclear if the differences between surveys were the result of the effects of seasonality, tropical storms, desiccation, some other physical parameters, or methodological differences.

--- SENTENCE 2234 ---
In general, the areas sampled showed no appreciable changes from 1975-1982, and the only marked change detected between surveys was the expansion of the seagrass beds (Halodule uninervis) adjacent to Cocos Island.

--- SENTENCE 2235 ---
However, there appears to have been a dramatic change in the marine plant communities in Cocos Lagoon in recent years.

--- SENTENCE 2236 ---
comm.) have reported that most of the seagrass in the lagoon died off approximately two years ago, and it has not returned.

--- SENTENCE 2237 ---
The cause of the die off is unknown, but locals speculate that disease or human factors, such as jet ski activity in shallow water or non-point source pollution, may have been responsible for the die-off (DAWR personnel pers.

--- SENTENCE 2238 ---
Virtually nothing is known of the algal communities on the banks in federal waters on Guam.

--- SENTENCE 2239 ---
However, Myers (1997) suggested that all of the 43 species that Tsuda (in Eldredge et al. 1977b) recorded on the submarine terrace and fore-reef slope in Agat Bay, are likely to occur in federal waters.

--- SENTENCE 2240 ---
Myers (1997) also noted that the only species that is regularly harvested commercially on Guam, *Gracilaria tsudai*, is unlikely to be present in federal waters, because it is associated with areas of nutrient enhancement by freshwater runoff or seepage.

## Algal Resources in CNMI

There is little information available on the status of the algal resources in CNMI, and most of the information that is available is not recent, restricted in distribution, or qualitative in nature.

--- SENTENCE 2241 ---
One example is the report by Amesbury et al. (1979), who described relative abundances of some algae in their survey of the fish resources of Saipan Lagoon in the 1970s.

--- SENTENCE 2242 ---
They reported that the patch reefs and the lagoonward fringe of the barrier reef were characterized by reef building coralline algae, while the submerged barrier reef supported a lush growth of *Chlorodesmis*.

--- SENTENCE 2243 ---
In contrast, the shallow sandy area in the north of the lagoon was characterized by a variety of algae including *Gracilaria edulis* and *Boergesenia forbesii*, while other sandy habitats contained scattered patches of *Sargassum polycystum* or were covered with the blue green algae *Microcoleus lyngbyaceus* (Amesbury et al. 1979).

--- SENTENCE 2244 ---
Areas where the substrate was composed of sand and rubble was also reported as supporting growths of *Padina*, *Caulerpa*, *Dictyota* and other algae, while areas dominated by patches of the seagrass *Halodule* supported a diverse assemblage of *Caulpera*.

--- SENTENCE 2245 ---
Another survey by Randall et al. (1985) in Tanapag Harbor on Saipan recorded a total of 45 species of marine plants in the area, which accounted for an overall mean algal cover of 23%.

--- SENTENCE 2246 ---
Randall et al. (1985) also reported that the marine plant communities varied with habitat zones.

--- SENTENCE 2247 ---
Sandy nearshore areas were characterised by species that were tolerant to salinity fluctuations, and which possessed modified attachment organs or sandbinding holdfasts (e.g. Halodule, Halophila and Halimeda macroloba).

--- SENTENCE 2248 ---
Species richness increased across the reef flat towards the reef margin.

--- SENTENCE 2249 ---
Gelidiopsis intricata, Boodlea composita, Microcoleus lyngbyaceus, Dictyosphaeria versluysii, Sphaecelaria versluysii and S. tribuloides were the dominant species of lagoon turf in the area.

--- SENTENCE 2250 ---
Most coralline species (especially Lithophyllum) seemed to grow well in areas of very strong or weak current.

--- SENTENCE 2251 ---
Randall et al. (1987) also completed a survey of the marine plants on the northern part of Tanapag reef platform.

--- SENTENCE 2252 ---
They recorded a total of 64 species in the study area, with patterns of distribution and abundance of marine plants similar to those described in Tanapag Harbor (Randall et al. 1985, 1987).

--- SENTENCE 2253 ---
Similarly, Randall et al. (1988) provided a brief description of the marine plants of Obyan Bay, Saipan.

--- SENTENCE 2254 ---
They recorded a total of 33 species in the area.

--- SENTENCE 2255 ---
Algal cover was highest in the outer zones of the reef platform (22-47%), with cover on the reef front varying from 20-38%.

--- SENTENCE 2256 ---
Dominant species in the inner moat included *Cladophoropsis* sp., *Gelidiopsis intricata*, *Sphacelaria*, and *Jania capillacea*.

--- SENTENCE 2257 ---
By comparison, *Turbinaria ornata* and *Neogoniolithon frutescens* were common on the outer platform, while *Liagora* sp. was common throughout the entire study area, especially on the reef front.

--- SENTENCE 2258 ---
A recent report by Wilkins et al. (1991) described the marine plant communities of Bahia Laulau and Tank Beach on Saipan in detail.

--- SENTENCE 2259 ---
They found that both of these bays have substantial algal diversity, including 95 species of algae and one species of seagrass (*Enhalus acoroides*).

--- SENTENCE 2260 ---
Wilkins et al. (1991) also described considerable seasonal variation in the cover and composition of the algae in the bay, which may have been the result of seasonal low tides and runoff from heavy rains.

--- SENTENCE 2261 ---
The patterns of variation in algal communities described in Bahia Laulau in this study were similar to those described in an earlier study of the bay by PBEC (1984).

--- SENTENCE 2262 ---
Very little is known about the algal communities of Tinian and Rota, although some information is available.

--- SENTENCE 2263 ---
PSDA (1997) reported that 84 species of marine plant have been recorded on the reefs adjacent to the beaches on Tinian (MRCPBEC 1994 in PSDA 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2264 ---
Similarly, limited surveys have reported 21 and 32 species of macroalgae on the reef flat along the northeast and southern coasts of Rota respectively (Randall & Smith 1988, Smith et al. 1989).

--- SENTENCE 2265 ---
Smith et al. (1989) also noted that macroalgal cover ranged from 3-87% on the reef flat on the south coast, while turf algal cover ranged from 34-87%.

--- SENTENCE 2266 ---
Some species (Laurencia sp. and Gracilaria sp.) were only found on the inner reef flat, while others (Ectocarpus breviartculatus, Gelidiella acerosa, and Asparagopsis taxiformis) were found only on the outer reef flat (Smith et al. 1989).

--- SENTENCE 2267 ---
Smith et al. (1989) also described the algal communities on the reef front on the south coast of Rota, where they recorded a total of 15 species.

--- SENTENCE 2268 ---
Macroalgal cover ranged from 36-39%, while turf algal cover ranged from 43-58% (Smith et al. 1989).

--- SENTENCE 2269 ---
The dominant algae were blue-greens (Schizothrix mexicana and Microcoleus lyngbyaceus), although green and red algae were also abundant (e.g. Halimeda opuntia, Amphiroa fragilissima, and Asparagopsis taxiformis: Smith et al. 1989).

--- SENTENCE 2270 ---
No brown algae were observed in the area (Smith et al. 1989).

--- SENTENCE 2271 ---
Several studies have also reported that the seagrass *Enhalus acoroides* has a limited distribution on Rota.

--- SENTENCE 2272 ---
This species has been recorded in narrow bands along the shore between the West Dock and Anjota Island near Songsong Village, and in the Talakhaya area along the southern coast (Smith et al. 1989, PSDA 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2273 ---
However, seagrass has not been observed in the West Dock area in recent years (J. Gourley pers.

--- SENTENCE 2274 ---
In contrast, well-developed seagrass beds dominate large areas of Saipan Lagoon (Eldredge 1983, Donaldson 1995, Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2275 ---
Information on the algal communities of the northern islands is sparse.

--- SENTENCE 2276 ---
Although an early survey by Eldredge et al. (1977a), provided some information on the marine benthic algal communities in Maug Lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 2277 ---
They found that these communities where characterized by low lying turfs comprised mostly of a mixture of red algae Gelidiopsis intricata, Tolypiocladia glomerulata, Jania capillacea and Polysiphonia sp., and the brown algae Lobophora variegata.

--- SENTENCE 2278 ---
At the time, these algae comprised 75-100% cover in the lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 2279 ---
With the exception of Asparagopsis taxiformis, all algal species were less than 5cm high, which the authors attributed to the high abundance of herbivorous fish in the lagoon (A. taxiformis is unpalatable to fishes because of its high iodine content:

--- SENTENCE 2280 ---
Eldredge et al 1977a).

--- SENTENCE 2281 ---
Eldredge et al. (1977a) also reported that the total number of algae species reported for the lagoon was 60 (approximately 30% of the species known from Guam), including Cyanophyta (4 spp.), Chlorophyta (25 spp.), Phaeophyta (11 spp.) and Rhodophyta (20 spp.)

--- SENTENCE 2282 ---
With the exception of one rare species (Laurencia succisa), all of these species had been previously recorded elsewhere in Micronesia (e.g. Guam).

--- SENTENCE 2283 ---
Eldredge et al (1977) suggested that the apparent absence of seagrasses and the larger Udotea species on Maug seems to support the idea that marine flora of the island shows closer similarity to Hawaii than to the southern Mariana Islands.

--- SENTENCE 2284 ---
More recently, Best (1984) described the macroalgae of the northern islands, and noted that with the exception of Pagan, few areas in the northern islands had exposed stands of noncalcified macroalgae.

--- SENTENCE 2285 ---
Best (1984) reported that a common intertidal zonation pattern was observed throughout the Northern Mariana Islands.

--- SENTENCE 2286 ---
An *Ectocarpus* zone was characteristically found at the high water mark, followed subtidally by bands of *Chnoospora* and *Turbinaria* (Best 1984).

--- SENTENCE 2287 ---
Best (1994) noted that these phaeophytes seemed to tenaciously persist in even the most wave exposed areas, which may provide a rare refuge from the abundant herbivorous fish populations.

--- SENTENCE 2288 ---
Conversely, macrochlorophytes were rare, possibly because of the high frequency of herbivorous fishes (Best 1984).

--- SENTENCE 2289 ---
The total number of species recorded on each of the northern islands in this survey was 48 at Pagan, 2 at Guguan, and 11 at Anatahan (Best 1994).

--- SENTENCE 2290 ---
In comparison, 21 species were recorded on each of two southern islands (Saipan and Aguijan: Best 1984).

--- SENTENCE 2291 ---
Hawaii

Hawaii's coral reefs support many species of marine algae or "seaweeds", which are currently under revision by Dr. I. Abbott and co-workers at the Botany Department, University of Hawaii.

--- SENTENCE 2292 ---
Over 450 species of marine algae have been described to date (470: see Eldredge & Miller 1995), although the total number of species recorded for Hawaii is likely to increase by another 40-50% (C. Smith pers.

--- SENTENCE 2293 ---
Five of the recorded species have been introduced to the islands (Eldredge & Miller 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2294 ---
Only one seagrass species, *Halophila hawaiiana*, occurs in the Hawaiian Islands, and it is endemic (Coles & Kuo 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2295 ---
Seaweeds or "limu" have long been used as food in Hawaii, and the ancient Hawaiians used them extensively in their diet (Magruder & Hunt 1979).

--- SENTENCE 2296 ---
It is thought that about 60-70 species of seaweed were once used by the Hawaiians (Fortner 1978, Magruder & Hunt 1979), although the number used now is around twenty, with less than ten commonly found in local fish markets (Magruder & Hunt 1979, Abbott 1988 in South 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2297 ---
Several species are still harvested for commercial and subsistence use in Hawaii, including *Gracilaria parvispora*, *Codium edule*, *Asparagopsis taxiformis* and *Ulva fasciata* (C. Smith pers.

--- SENTENCE 2298 ---
The most valuable, *Gracilaria*, has annual sales in Hawaii of at least US\$80,000 (South 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2299 ---
In addition to human consumption, seaweeds are also used as a source of extracted chemicals (see above), and Santos and Doty (1985: in Moss & Doty 1987) listed 1,047 natural algal products that could be found in Hawaii seaweeds and identified the species from which they could be obtained.

--- SENTENCE 2300 ---
Santelices and Doty (1989) reported that the standing stock of *Gracilaria* in tropical latitudes is low, and does not usually exceed 2 kg/m² (Santelices & Doty 1989).

--- SENTENCE 2301 ---
Unfortunately, the current status of populations of commercial algae species in Hawaii is unknown, although it appears that *G. parvispora* has almost been eliminated from Oahu (Hunt et al. 1982, C. Smith pers.

--- SENTENCE 2302 ---
Most of the information on the algae of the MHI has come from nearshore reefs in state waters.

--- SENTENCE 2303 ---
However, there is some information available for Penguin Bank.

--- SENTENCE 2304 ---
Agegian & Abbott (1985 in Friedlander 1996) investigated the deepwater macroalgal community on Penguin Bank using a manned submersible.

--- SENTENCE 2305 ---
They reported that the bank consists of a broad carbonate platform (~60m deep), is covered with loose carbonate rubble and coarse sediments from the calcareous green alga, *Halimeda* (Friedlander 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2306 ---
They also noted that the algal community on the bank contained 54 species (8 brown species, 16 green species, and 30 red species), and was characterized by two deepwater species (*Codium mamillosum* and *Lithothamnium* sp.) and many species that occur in shallow water (primarily *Lobophora variegata*, *Dictyota friabilis*, and *Peysonellia rubra*: see Friedlander 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2307 ---
The deeper areas of the bank (182m) were dominated by crustose coralline algae (see Friedlander 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2308 ---
Some information is also available for the NWHI.

--- SENTENCE 2309 ---
A reexamination of previous collections and analysis of recent collections have resulted in the recognition of 205 species for the NWHI, including a number of new deepwater species relatively unknown in the area (Abbott 1989 in Friedlander 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2310 ---
Species recorded from the NWHI now include 48 taxa of green algae

(Chlorophyta: 8 new records for the NWHI), 33 taxa of brown algae (Phaeophyta: 7 new records for the NWHI), and 124 species of red algae (Rhodophyta: 26 new records for the NWHI) (Abbott 1989 in Friedlander 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2311 ---
An earlier study of the nearshore fishery resources of the NWHI recorded a total of 101 species in the area (Okamoto & Kawamoto 1980 in Friedlander 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2312 ---
Five, of which, were common to all islands (see Friedlander 1995): two greens (Caulerpa racemosa and Dictyospaeria versluysii) and three reds (Jania spp., Porolithon gardneri and P. onkodes).

--- SENTENCE 2313 ---

--- SENTENCE 2314 ---

## 2.5.4 Other U.S. Pacific Islands

The algal resources of the Other U.S. Pacific Islands have not been well studied, although the numbers of species on these islands and atolls are likely to range between 100 and 300 (USFWS 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2326 ---
Previous surveys of Johnston and Palmyra have recorded 93 and 88 species at these two locations respectively, although this is considered to be an underestimate (Cooke 1986).

--- SENTENCE 2327 ---
Species recorded at Johnston include 23 species of green algae, 9 species of brown algae, 41 species of red algae and 19 species of blue-green algae (USFWS 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2328 ---
A survey of the algae at Johnston Atoll in the 1980s showed that the most abundant species were Caulerpa serrulata, C. racemosa, Dictyosphaeria sp., Halimeda sp., Calothrix/Microcoleus sp., Bryopsis pennata, and several types of coralline algae (purple, brown and yellow: Irons et al. 1984).

--- SENTENCE 2329 ---
Irons et al. (1984) also showed that the relative abundance of these species varied among 12 different "ecotypes" or zones on the atoll (described in Corals and "Live Rock").

--- SENTENCE 2330 ---
Two of these Zones (8 and 9) were located in federal waters, where algal cover and diversity were high relative to nearshore areas (see Corals and "Live Rock").

--- SENTENCE 2331 ---
The most abundant species in Zone 8, in order of abundance, were Caulerpa serrulata, Halimeda sp., Calothrix/Microcoleus sp. and purple coralline algae (Irons et al. 1984).

--- SENTENCE 2332 ---
In contrast, the most abundant species in Zone 9, in order of abundance, were purple coralline algae, Caulerpa racemosa, Calothrix/Microcoleus sp., C. serrulata and Halimeda sp. (Irons et al. 1984).

--- SENTENCE 2333 ---
No information is available on the algal resources located on the other atolls.

--- SENTENCE 2334 ---
## 2.6 Non-consumptive Resources

Coral reefs provide an important natural resource for non-extractive purposes such as tourism or recreation by local people (Maragos et al 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2335 ---
Both tourists and residents enjoy water activities including diving, snorkeling or viewing from a boat or submersible, where they can observe reef fishes and invertebrates in their natural environment (Clark 1991, Smith 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2336 ---
All of the states and territories in the U.S. Pacific Islands have extensive coral reefs that provide high quality destinations for tourism and recreation, although tourism is developed to different degrees in each location as follows:

## 2.6.1 American Samoa

American Samoa's tourist industry is small relative to the other states and territories.

--- SENTENCE 2337 ---
The most current and best source of visitor use data for American Samoa is contained in the October 1994 "Report to the Governor and 5-Year Tourism Action Plan", which was recently summarized by the National Parks Service (NPS 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2338 ---
In 1993, less than 5,000 tourists visited American Samoa, not counting an estimated 5,000 cruise-ship passengers whose stay rarely exceeds eight hours (NPS 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2339 ---
These numbers are considerably lower than those of 20 yrs ago (NPS 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2340 ---
In the peak year (1974), more than 35,000 tourist came to the Territory.

--- SENTENCE 2341 ---
Since then, there has been a steady decline in the number of tourists, probably because of a decline in air service, deterioration of the primary hotel (the Rainmaker), competition in the region, population explosion and environmental degradation, and inadequate tourism management and lack of funding (NPS 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2342 ---
At present, most of the tourists come from the United States, followed by

New Zealand, Europe and Australia.

--- SENTENCE 2343 ---
The average length of stay of tourists in American Samoa is short (about four days: NPS 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2344 ---
The recently dedicated National Park of American Samoa is considered to be a great opportunity for increasing tourism in the area (NPS 1996), and coral reefs are considered to be an important draw card for the park.

--- SENTENCE 2345 ---
In this context, the shallow lagoon in the National Park at Ofu warrants special mention.

--- SENTENCE 2346 ---
The coral reef communities in this lagoon are in exceptionally good condition, being characterised by high coral cover, spectacular coral microatolls, and a rich and abundant fish fauna (Hunter et al. 1993, Green 1996a).

--- SENTENCE 2347 ---
Giant clams are also more abundant in this lagoon than they are anywhere else in the Territory except at Rose Atoll (Green & Craig 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2348 ---
This, in combination with the calm and protected waters inside the lagoon, provides the best opportunity for non-consumptive use in the Territory (eg. snorkeling: Hunter et al. 1993, Green 1996a).

--- SENTENCE 2349 ---
In addition to tourism, local people also use the reefs of American Samoa extensively for recreation (mostly fishing and swimming in front of villages).

--- SENTENCE 2350 ---
It is not known how much recreational activity takes place in federal waters.

--- SENTENCE 2351 ---
However, it is assumed that almost all recreation and tourism takes place on the nearshore, shallow reefs in territorial waters where the reefs are most accessible.

--- SENTENCE 2352 ---
## 2.6.2 CNMI

Tourism is the primary industry in CNMI, and Saipan is the main destination, receiving about 97% of the 722,028 visitors to the Commonwealth in 1996 (MVB Visitor Arrival Statistics 1995-1996).

--- SENTENCE 2353 ---
Tourism is also rapidly increasing, with the total number of tourists visiting Saipan each year increasing from 430,000 in 1991 to 703,000 in 1996 (GVB 1995, MVB Visitor Arrival Statistics 1995-1996).

--- SENTENCE 2354 ---
Visitor expenditures are also increasing rapidly, ranging from \$61 million in 1980 to \$422 million in 1990 (CRMDEQ 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2355 ---
More recently Gourley (1997) reported that the total revenue for visitors entering CNMI in 1996 was \$575.8 million.

--- SENTENCE 2356 ---
Japanese tourists make up most of the visitors to CNMI (63%), with lesser numbers coming from elsewhere in Asia (eg. 18% from Korea), Micronesia and the U.S (GVB 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2357 ---
Marine resources play an important role in the tourism industry in the Northern Marianas, since most visitors list "beautiful seas" and water sports as their primary motivation for visiting the island (GVB 1995, see *Guam* below).

--- SENTENCE 2358 ---
Island residents also use the reefs and adjacent beach parks regularly for recreation.

--- SENTENCE 2359 ---
Much of the tourism industry in CNMI is concentrated on Saipan, especially around Saipan Lagoon and the war memorials in the north.

--- SENTENCE 2360 ---
However, Laulau Bay is also heavily used by both tourists and residents for fishing, boating, swimming, sunbathing and picnicking (PBEC 1984).

--- SENTENCE 2361 ---
Tourism is also increasing on the small island of Rota, and is likely to increase on Tinian when the new casino is built at San Jose.

--- SENTENCE 2362 ---
Diving is an important industry in CNMI, generating \$15.6 million per year of gross income on Saipan alone (DEQ in prep.).

--- SENTENCE 2363 ---
The most heavily used dive sites on Saipan include Laulau Bay on the southeast coast, Obyan on the south coast, and the Grotto on the northeast coast (J. Comfort

pers.

--- SENTENCE 2364 ---
comm., DEQ in prep.).

--- SENTENCE 2365 ---
Recently, DEQ (in prep.) estimated that there may be more than 84,000 dives done in Laulau Bay alone each year.

--- SENTENCE 2366 ---
Dive boats from Saipan also go over to Tinian (weather permitting: J. Comfort pers.

--- SENTENCE 2367 ---
comm.), and there is a small, but thriving dive industry on Rota.

--- SENTENCE 2368 ---
Unfortunately, one of the prime dive sites on Rota was damaged severely last year, when the military detonated unexploded ordinance in a Sasanhaya Bay (see *Military Activities*).

--- SENTENCE 2369 ---
As the federal position is that it has jurisdiction up to the shoreline in CNMI (see Hunter 1995), all tourism and recreation on coral reefs in CNMI takes places in federal waters.

### 2.6.3

--- SENTENCE 2370 ---
Guam

Tourism is a rapidly growing multi-million dollar industry on Guam (GVB 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2371 ---
The number of visitors to Guam each year has increased dramatically over the last decade from 400,000 in 1986 to 1,300,000 in 1995 and 1996 (GVB 1995, unpubl. data).

--- SENTENCE 2372 ---
Most of the visitors (74%) are from Japan, with the rest coming from elsewhere in Asia, Micronesia and the U.S. (GVB 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2373 ---
Tourism is a major employer in Guam, with a total of 46,000 people employed in the industry in 1995 (GVB 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2374 ---
In 1996, the industry collected over \$26 million in hotel occupancy tax alone (GVB unpubl. data).

--- SENTENCE 2375 ---
In 1996, the total expenditure by each tourist was estimated to be \$1,143 (Birkeland 1997b).

--- SENTENCE 2376 ---
Given that 1.3 million tourists visited the island in 1996, tourist expenditure for Guam that year was in the order of \$1,486 million.

--- SENTENCE 2377 ---
Marine resources play an important role in the tourism industry on Guam, since most visitors (49-80%) list "beautiful seas" and water sports (including fishing, diving, seawalking, and observing marine life from the submarine and fisheye marine park) as their primary motivation for visiting the island (GVB 1995, Aguon 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2378 ---
Moreover, Birkeland (1997b) noted that approximately 10% of the tourists come to Guam specifically for the diving.

--- SENTENCE 2379 ---
Given the average expenditure of each visitor per trip, Birkeland (1997b) estimated that diving alone accounts for at least \$148.6 million dollars of the tourist expenditure on Guam each year.

--- SENTENCE 2380 ---
Local dive operators report that the most popular dive sites on Guam are on the western side of the island, because they are the most accessible (J. Bent pers.

--- SENTENCE 2381 ---
These include: Apra Harbor (Western Shoal, Finger Reef and the Wrecks), Blue Hole and "The Crevice" on the southwestern side of Orote Peninsula, Anigua Reef, Double Reef and Palau Wall on the northwestern side (J. Bent pers.

--- SENTENCE 2382 ---
The reefs on the south and eastern side are also good dive sites, but they are not dived as frequently because of weather constraints (J. Bent pers.

--- SENTENCE 2383 ---
The commercial dive industry on Guam supports three main groups of divers: Japanese tourists or TAIKAN divers, local divers, and military recreational divers (J. Bent pers.

--- SENTENCE 2384 ---
Each group tends to utilize different sites around the island (J. Bent pers.

--- SENTENCE 2385 ---
In general, the TAIKAN divers are the most numerous (100's a day) and least experienced, and they are taken to safe locations where there is not much coral to damage (eg. Family Beach and Outhouse Beach in Apra Harbor, Power Station Channel, and Piti Bomb Hole: J. Bent pers.

--- SENTENCE 2386 ---
In contrast, the local divers and military recreational divers tend to be more experienced and cause less damage of the reefs (but see *Tourism and Recreation*), and they tend to go to the more advanced dive sites (J. Bent pers.

--- SENTENCE 2387 ---
All activities associated with tourism and recreation take place within nearshore territorial waters in Guam.

## 2.6.4 Hawaii

After 40 years of spectacular growth in mass tourism, Hawaii's tourist industry is the largest industry in Hawaii, providing about 40% of the gross state product and a third of the direct jobs, income and government revenue (Liu & Auyong 1988).

--- SENTENCE 2388 ---
Secondary benefits of tourism are also likely to exceed these direct benefits (Liu 1986 in Liu & Auyong 1988).

--- SENTENCE 2389 ---
A study by Liu & Auyong (1988) reported that the visitor count to Hawaii in 1986 was in excess of 5.6 million (6 visitors to every resident), and that the total was predicted to increase to 8 million by the year 2000 (Liu et al 1987 in Liu & Auyong 1988).

--- SENTENCE 2390 ---
In 1988, the Hawaii Visitors Bureau estimated that the total visitor expenditures for that year were \$9.2 billion (Clark 1991).

--- SENTENCE 2391 ---
Hawaii's ocean resources, including coral reefs, play an important role in the tourist industry, since 85% of visitors participated in some form of ocean recreation (see Clark 1991).

--- SENTENCE 2392 ---
Several studies found that the most desirable strategy for the development of a long-term quality destination for tourism in Hawaii is through outdoor recreation, and marine resources play a critical role in this development (see Liu & Auyong 1988).

--- SENTENCE 2393 ---
Outdoor recreation is a favorite leisure activity for Hawaii's residents, and coral reefs are central to the \$700 million marine recreation industry (Grigg 1997b).

--- SENTENCE 2394 ---
Hawaii's ocean recreation industry is rapidly expanding, and revenues generated from these activities have quadrupled over the past decade, from \$128 million in 1981 to \$560 million in 1992 (see Clark 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2395 ---
Based on 1985 State Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan (CSORP) statistics, at least 170, 000 people swim at beaches or shorelines on a typically busy day (Clark 1991).

--- SENTENCE 2396 ---
Seaward of the shoreline, other forms of ocean recreation are being enjoyed: some 23,000 people are surfing, 25,000 are fishing, 3,000 are paddling canoes or kayaks, 18,000 are enjoying other kinds of boating, and 21,000 people are diving (Clark 1991).

--- SENTENCE 2397 ---
Total revenues from the SCUBA industry alone were 26.9 million in 1990 (A. Clark pers.

--- SENTENCE 2398 ---
com. in Hunter 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2399 ---
Almost all of the tourism and recreation involving coral reefs in Hawaii takes place in the readily accessible, nearshore state waters in the MHI (HOMRC 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2400 ---
In some locations, such as Hanauma Bay on Oahu, the use of coral reefs for tourism and recreation is intensive (DOH 1992).

--- SENTENCE 2401 ---
However, some recreational dive groups do visit reefs in the federal waters in the MHI

also, including Penquin Bank.

--- SENTENCE 2402 ---
Kaula Rock is also visited by recreational divers, but rarely because of its isolation.

--- SENTENCE 2403 ---
In general, most of the reefs in the NWHI are unsuitable for non-consumptive use, because they are too remote, subject to seasonably poor weather conditions, closed to visitation, or the water depth is too great (Friedlander 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2404 ---
One exception is Midway Atoll, where a tourism industry has recently been established (Friedlander 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2405 ---
Eco-tourism plays an important role in the tourism industry at Midway, and non-consumptive uses of the marine environment include SCUBA diving and snorkeling (Friedlander 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2406 ---
However, these activities are expected to be minimal, because of poor winter weather and the type of visitors that the island is expected to attract, such as educational groups (eg. elder hostel groups), natural history tours (primarily bird watchers) and recreational fishermen (B. Flint pers.

--- SENTENCE 2407 ---
comm.)

## 2.6.5 Other U.S. Pacific Islands

The pristine coral reefs on the remote atolls and islands have considerable coral reef resources, which would be highly valued for tourism and recreation.

--- SENTENCE 2408 ---
However, most of these islands are not amenable to this type of use because they are either too remote or closed to visitation by the general public because they are occupied by the military or sensitive areas for wildlife conservation (eg. National Wildlife Refuges).

--- SENTENCE 2409 ---
Palmyra requires permission in advance to visit from its private owners.

--- SENTENCE 2410 ---
However, some of these reefs may be visited occasionally by yacht crews cruising the Pacific Islands.

--- SENTENCE 2411 ---
The exception to this rule is Johnston Atoll, which is occupied by the military, who use the reefs for recreation, including fishing, swimming, diving and snorkeling.

## III.

--- SENTENCE 2412 ---
PATTERNS OF UTILIZATION

The inhabitants of the Pacific Islands utilize their coral reef resources in different ways, depending on the natural resources that are available and local customs and available fishing equipment.

--- SENTENCE 2413 ---
Overall, reef fin-fish are thought to account for 50-60% of the total nearshore fisheries landings in the Pacific Islands (Dalzell & Adams 1994 in Dalzell & Adams in press), and simple models predict Maximum Sustainable Yields (MSYs) for reef finfish in this region ranging from 4.5-20 t/km²/yr (Dalzell & Adams in press).

--- SENTENCE 2414 ---
The annual nominal fisheries production for the Pacific Islands, including the WPRFMC region, has recently been summarized by Dalzell, Adams & co-workers (see Table 47).

--- SENTENCE 2415 ---
They reported that most of the catch in American Samoa, Guam and CNMI came from the subsistence fisheries (81%, 80% and 95% respectively), while the opposite was true in Hawaii where most of the catch (84%) was recorded from the commercial fisheries (Table 47).

--- SENTENCE 2416 ---
Reef and deep slope fish comprised only a small proportion of the commercial catch in American Samoa, Guam and Hawaii (16%, 8% and 13% respectively: Table 47).

--- SENTENCE 2417 ---
In contrast, reef and deep slope fish comprised almost half (47%) of the commercial catch in CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 2418 ---
Reef invertebrates comprised only a minor proportion of the commercial catch in each location (0.1-4.2%: Table 47).

--- SENTENCE 2419 ---
No breakdown of the data was presented for the subsistence fisheries.

## 3.1 American Samoa

The islands of American Samoa are partially surrounded by narrow fringing reefs, the tops of which are exposed at low tide (Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2437 ---
The reef flat and adjacent shallow waters are inhabited by a diverse array of fish and shellfish species that are harvested by local residents on an almost daily basis throughout the year (see Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2438 ---
These fisheries are considered highly productive, yielding up to 65 tons of biomass per square mile (Wass 1980 in US Congress 1987).

--- SENTENCE 2439 ---
More recently, Dalzell and Adams (in press) predicted that the estimated MSY for reef finfish in American Samoa was likely to be in the vicinity of 20 t/km²/yr.

--- SENTENCE 2440 ---
The coral reef fishery has two components: the shoreline subsistence fishery and the boat-based artisanal fishery.

--- SENTENCE 2441 ---
The American Samoa Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources (DMWR) has been monitoring these fisheries since the 1970s, and the results are described below.

--- SENTENCE 2442 ---
At this point it should be noted that the use of the terms commercial, subsistence or recreational can not

<sup>&</sup>lt;sup>3</sup> "Nominal value" is the total value if all components of the catch, including subsistence landings, were sold at current local market prices (Adams & Dalzell in press).

be strictly applied to the fisheries in American Samoa, because some fish are sold and others are retained for personal use in each fishery (Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2443 ---
For example, approximately 25% of the shoreline subsistence fishery is sold (Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2444 ---
## 3.1.1 Shoreline Subsistence Fishery

Domestic fisheries in American Samoa landed 587,000 lb. of fish and invertebrates in 1991 worth approximately \$993,000 on the local market (Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2445 ---
The majority of which (78% by catch and 80% by value) was taken by the shoreline subsistence fishery (Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2446 ---
This fishery occurs entirely on the coral reefs surrounding the islands in territorial waters.

--- SENTENCE 2447 ---
Most of the shoreline fishery is made up of individuals on foot who fish in areas adjacent to their villages (Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2448 ---
Principal methods used in 1991 were rod and reel (37%), handline (25%), free diving (14), gill netting (9%), gleaning (8%) and throw netting (5%: Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2449 ---
The average catch per unit effort (CPUE) was 3 lb/gear-hour, although CPUE varied among gear types from 0.7lb./gear-hour for bamboo pole hook and line to 12.2 lb./gear-hour for gill nets (Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2450 ---
In 1991, the island-wide subsistence catch on Tutuila Island was 439,000 lb., which was worth an estimated \$768,000 on the local market (based on an average rate of \$1.75/lb.:

--- SENTENCE 2451 ---
Ponwith 1992, Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2452 ---
Expanding these data to include limited catches in the Manu'a Islands produces a total subsistence catch of 456,000 lb. for the Territory, worth an estimated \$798,000 (Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2453 ---
However, the dollar value of this fishery does not adequately represent the high economic and social importance of the resource, because of the subsistence component of Samoan culture and the generally low wage scale received by islanders that are employed (Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2454 ---
Virtually all fish and invertebrates species caught in this fishery are retained for consumption or sale.

--- SENTENCE 2455 ---
In 1991, 69 taxa were harvested (Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2456 ---
Fishes accounted for 86% of the total catch by weight, with most of the catch composition (46%) accounted for by the migratory atule (Selar crumenophthalmus: Table 48).

--- SENTENCE 2457 ---
The majority of the reef species taken were jacks, surgeonfishes, mullet and octopus (Table 48).

--- SENTENCE 2458 ---
Fish sizes were surprisingly small, particularly for groupers and snappers that had very low mean weights (0.3-0.4 pound: Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2459 ---
Some favored species, such as giant clams, were generally absent in the catch because of overharvesting (Craig et al. 1993, see Overfishing).

--- SENTENCE 2460 ---
One unique species taken was a burrowing polychaete, the palolo worm Eunice viridis.

--- SENTENCE 2461 ---
Palolo emerge once or twice a year at predictable times to release their reproductive segments (epitokes) into the nearshore waters (Caspers 1984).

--- SENTENCE 2462 ---
Samoans consider these epitokes a delicacy and gather them using scoop nets or long lengths of screen (Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2463 ---
Palolo catches are highly variable (3,400 lb in 1990 and 600 lb in 1991), probably due to variation in the strength of the spawning event and prevailing weather conditions (Ponwith 1992).

--- SENTENCE 2464 ---
Catch composition of the shoreline subsistence fishery on Tutuila Island in 1991 (from Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2500 ---
Local sources also reveal that most of the seaweed or "limu" eaten in American Samoa is imported from Western Samoa (S. Saucerman and P. Craig pers.

--- SENTENCE 2501 ---
At present, DMWR has no information regarding coral or "live rock" collecting in the Territory (S. Saucerman pers.

--- SENTENCE 2502 ---
Coral collecting is banned at depths of less than 60 ft (Hunter 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2503 ---
However, it is allowed at depths of more than 60 ft, but only with a permit from DMWR (Hunter 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2504 ---
Long-term monitoring by DMWR has shown that this fishery appears to have been in decline since the 1970s (Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2505 ---
Ponwith (1992) reported that there was a major decrease (~54%) in the adjusted island-wide catch of reef-resident species (excluding atule) over a period of 12 years from 1979 to 1991, while effort decreased by only 8% (see Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2506 ---
Similarly, Saucerman (1995) has shown that this fishery continued to decline from 1991 to 1994, with a 70% decline in total catch, a 30% decline in effort, and a 60% decline in CPUE.

--- SENTENCE 2507 ---
Notable exceptions to the apparent decline in effort are the fisheries for two highly prized species, atule and palolo (Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2508 ---
The decline in the inshore subsistence fishery could be due to a number of factors.

--- SENTENCE 2509 ---
For example, it could be the result of a decline in the resource, possibly due to habitat degradation caused by a combination of natural and anthropogenic effects (Craig et al. 1993, Saucerman 1995, see *Coral Reef Communities* and *Sedimentation*).

--- SENTENCE 2510 ---
Alternatively, the decline may be the result of sociological changes associated with a shift from a subsistence to a market economy, where people no longer have as much time or incentive to fish (Craig et al. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 2511 ---
Craig et al. (1993) also suggested that overexploitation may have resulted in the decline of the fishery for at least one target species, giant clams (see *Overfishing*).

--- SENTENCE 2512 ---
It is likely that a combination of these factors have played a role in the decline in this fishery.

--- SENTENCE 2513 ---
## 3.1.2 Boat Based Fisheries

DMWR has been collecting commercial fisheries statistics from the local fleet on Tutuila since the early 1970's and from the Manu'a Islands since 1983.

--- SENTENCE 2514 ---
Most data collected over the years have been from the commercial fleet, but beginning in October 1985, DMWR's data collection programs were modified to include data on recreational and subsistence fisheries as well (Hamm et al. 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2515 ---
Data from this survey are summarized each year in the "Fishery Statistics of the Western Pacific" which is prepared by the Western Pacific Fisheries Information Network (WPaCFIN) staff at the National Marine Fisheries Service in Honolulu (Hamm et al. 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2516 ---
The following fisheries statistics were summarized for 1993 by Hamm et al. (1995).

--- SENTENCE 2517 ---
The domestic boat based fisheries of American Samoa are typically small boat, one-day fisheries, and the majority of the fleet is composed of 28- to 29-foot outboard engine powered catamarans (Hamm et al. 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2518 ---
During 1993, 43 boats were sampled, 32 from Tutuila and 11 from the Manu'a Islands (Hamm et al. 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2519 ---
Most of the fishing was done by trolling and bottomfishing, and the majority of the catch was sold locally (Hamm et al. 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2520 ---
During 1993, on average,

trips on boats from Tutuila had three-man crews, fished 112 hours, and caught about 160 pounds of fish, while those from the Manu'a Islands had 3.4 man crews, fished 5 hours and caught about 110 pounds of fish (Hamm et al. 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2521 ---
A total of 443 lb of reef fish were landed by the commercial boat based fishery in American Samoa in 1993, which was only a minor proportion (<1%) of the total landings for that year (Table 50).

--- SENTENCE 2522 ---
However, several species that were classified as bottomfish by Hamm et al. (1994) can also be considered reef fish, and they accounted for another 7,256 lb landed (value=\$12,499) or 10% of the total catch (Table 50).

--- SENTENCE 2523 ---
Therefore, the combined total catch and value of reef fish in this fishery is small (1,942 lb and \$13,207).

--- SENTENCE 2524 ---
It is unclear how much, if any, of this fishery occurs in the EEZ.

--- SENTENCE 2525 ---
However, Craig et al. (1993) reported that no major commercial fishery operates in federal waters in American Samoa.

## **3.1.3 Summary**

Mean total fisheries landings in American Samoa over the last few years (1991 to 1995) was 544,284 lb, which was valued at \$887,474 on the local market (Table 52).

--- SENTENCE 2558 ---
Coral reef fisheries accounted for approximately 62% of the catch and 70% of the value over time (Table 52).

--- SENTENCE 2559 ---
The actual total for coral reef fisheries is probably higher than this, since it will include an unknown proportion of the bottomfish catch also (see *Boat Based Fishery* above).

--- SENTENCE 2560 ---
It should also be noted that these figures do not include the shoreline artisanal catch, which is assumed to be substantial (P. Craig pers.

--- SENTENCE 2561 ---
Most of the landings in the known coral reef fisheries in American Samoa are reef fishes (64%) and molluscs (22%: Table 52).

--- SENTENCE 2562 ---
Smaller amounts of crustaceans (2%) and echinoderms (13%) are also harvested (Table 52), and a small, but unknown, harvest of seaweeds occurs (see *Shoreline Subsistence Fishery* above).

--- SENTENCE 2563 ---
Coral and live rock harvesting have not been reported in the Territory (see *Shoreline Subsistence Fishery* above).

--- SENTENCE 2575 ---
However, Craig et al. (1993) reported that no major commercial fishery operates in federal waters in American Samoa.

--- SENTENCE 2578 ---

--- SENTENCE 2579 ---

## **3.2 CNMI**

The reef fishery in CNMI is primarily limited to nearshore (≤3 nmi) fringing or barrier reef systems in the southern islands (Saipan, Tinian and Rota: Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2588 ---
Although a limited amount of fishing does occur on offshore reefs (>3 nmi: Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2589 ---
Gourley (1997) suggested that Tinian and Rota appear to fit the general Pacific Island reef fisheries model proposed by Dalzell et al. (1996).

--- SENTENCE 2590 ---
This model suggests that reef fisheries are "overwhelmingly" subsistence in nature, with only about 20% of the fish and invertebrates taken from the local coral reef fishery entering the commercial market.

--- SENTENCE 2591 ---
Tinian and Rota appear to fit this model because they have a relatively small local population and an insignificant tourist industry (Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2592 ---
In contrast, Saipan does not appear to fit this model since it has a huge market for fresh seafood generated by its large resident population and substantial tourist industry (Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2593 ---
Radtke and Davis (1995 in Gourley 1997) estimated that the amount of seafood purchased annually for consumer sale in CNMI might approach \$11 million, based on a daily population of 65,000 people (including residents and tourists).

--- SENTENCE 2594 ---
Frequently, the demand outweighs the local supply, and 677,614 lb of fish products were imported into the Commonwealth in 1993, most of which (80%) came from the Philippines and the Republic of Palau (Radtke & Davis 1995 in Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2595 ---
An increase in the volume of imported reef fish was also noted during 1994 (see Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2596 ---
According to data obtained from Airway Bills, most of these reef fish imports came from other Pacific Islands (Hamm et al. 1996 in Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2597 ---
The coral reef fisheries in CNMI will be described over two time frames.

--- SENTENCE 2598 ---
First, the history of the fisheries will be described; and second, a summary of the recent fishery statistics will be provided.

--- SENTENCE 2599 ---
Historical information on the fisheries in CNMI go back as far as pre-World War II (WWII) and were summarized by Uchida (1983).

--- SENTENCE 2600 ---
Prior to WWII, the Japanese exploited many coral reef resources in the Japanese Mandated Islands (JMI), which included CNMI (Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2601 ---
The Japanese attempted culturing the black-lip pearl oysters (*Pinctada margaritifera*) on Saipan, but eventually concentrated most of their efforts in Palau (Smith 1947a in Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2602 ---
Five species of sea cucumbers were exploited to produce trepang or beche-de-mer in Saipan, with a catch of 54, 284 kg of sea cucumbers recorded in 1941, which had a dollar value \$6,678 (Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2603 ---
The Japanese also started an industry for trochus shells in Saipan, by transplanting *Trochus niloticus* to the island from Palau (see Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2604 ---
No shell production records are available, but the industry was said to have been successful (see Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2605 ---
Exploitation of reef fishes was also reported prior to WWII when many species of reef fish were used as bait for tuna fishing in the Japanese Mariana Islands (JMI: Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2606 ---
In the course of WWII, almost all of the fishery bases that were developed by the Japanese in the JMI were destroyed (Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2607 ---
Following WWII, fishing was an important daily activity in CNMI, and the Saipan islanders consumed nearly 0.45 kg of fish per person per day and there was a steady market for fishery products (Smith 1947b in Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2608 ---
However fishing remained a subsistence-type activity and never developed to any extent in CNMI in the post-war years (Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2609 ---
Several attempts were made to establish a commercial fishery after the war, but they all failed (Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2610 ---
However, fishing was recognized as having a major potential for economic growth in the Mariana (Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2611 ---
By the 1970s, there had been a resurgence of interest and the multispecies fishery in the Marianas had grown to include about 70 full-time and 90-100 part-time commercial fishermen with about 120 small boats (most < 6m).

--- SENTENCE 2612 ---
Most of these fishermen made short trips and returned each day by early afternoon to sell their catch before dark, although some of the larger vessels made longer trips to the northern islands (see Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2613 ---
Data from the Department of Natural Resources (DNR) indicates the that landings of reef fishes was very variable from 1975-1978 (2,197 kg, 5,381 kg, 17,970 kg and 2,804 kg recorded in 1975, 1976, 1977 and 1978 respectively: see Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2614 ---
The estimated value of this fishery was an average of \$10,938 per year from 1975-1978, although these figures were assumed to be a gross underestimate (Uchida 1983).

--- SENTENCE 2615 ---
At this time, Uchida (1983 in Gourley 1997) noted that while certain species and species groups were locally important in the fishery, the inshore fishery resources of CNMI were considered inadequate to support a sustainable export business, with the possible exception of atulai.

--- SENTENCE 2616 ---
(1974 in Gourley 1997) also described the fishery on Tinian in the 1970s, based on a limited survey of local fishermen.

--- SENTENCE 2617 ---
They interviewed only three local fishermen who made more than 50% of their annual income from fishing.

--- SENTENCE 2618 ---
However, numerous others interviewed in San Jose village were considered part-time commercial fishermen (<50% of annual income) or subsistence fishermen.

--- SENTENCE 2619 ---
Fishing for recreational purposes was not mentioned.

--- SENTENCE 2620 ---
Interviews with local villagers found that most reef fishermen went spearfishing from the shoreline at night, mostly on the leeward coast.

--- SENTENCE 2621 ---
Species groups targeted on Tinian included acanthurids, holocentrids, kyphosids, labrids, lutjanids, mullids, scarids, serranids, and siganids.

--- SENTENCE 2622 ---
In comparison, there was limited fishing effort directed towards trolling for pelagic species (mahi mahi, skipjack tuna, wahoo, yellowfin tuna, and barracuda).

--- SENTENCE 2623 ---
This was probably because it was difficult to land whole fish by trolling, because of the substantial local shark population in the area.

--- SENTENCE 2624 ---
In recent years, there have been some dramatic changes in the demography of the human population in CNMI (CRMDEQ 1995), which seem to be affecting the local fisheries.

--- SENTENCE 2625 ---
The population has increased from 16,780 to 43,345 in just ten years (from 1980 to 1990), and most of the population (90%) live on Saipan (CRMDEQ 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2626 ---
This dramatic increase has been primarily due to an influx of non-resident "alien" workers (non-resident work permits increased from 2,866 in 1980 to 22,745 in 1990: CRMDEQ 1995), who come to Saipan to work in the garment factories and the tourism business (J. Gourley pers.

--- SENTENCE 2627 ---
A total of 53.7% of the people in CNMI are now non-U.S. citizens, mostly from the Philippines and China (CRMDEQ 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2628 ---
Conversely, there has been a dramatic decline in the percentage of indigenous people in the population (from 70.3% in 1980 to 34.4% in 1990: CRMDEQ 1995).

--- SENTENCE 2629 ---
The influx of Asian workers appears to have changed the nature of the coral reef fisheries on Saipan.

--- SENTENCE 2630 ---
For example, Gourley (pers.

--- SENTENCE 2631 ---
com.) noted that Asian fishermen are now represented in all sectors of the nearshore fishery.

--- SENTENCE 2632 ---
Many of the Asian fishermen, especially Filipinos, fish for both subsistence and recreation (J. Gourley and J. Furey pers.

--- SENTENCE 2633 ---
In addition, many of the fishermen working for the commercial fishing operations are now alien workers (mostly Filipinos and some people from the FSM: J. Gourley, V. Benavente, C. La Plante and J. Palacios pers.

--- SENTENCE 2634 ---
Similarly, most of the fish at the road-side market are caught and sold by Filipino fishermen (unidentified local fishermen pers.

--- SENTENCE 2635 ---
Asian workers also do most of the gleaning on Saipan, and there appears to have been an increase in gleaning on the island over the last 10-15 years (J. Gourley and J. Furey pers.

--- SENTENCE 2636 ---
Moreover, there has been a change in the species that are being harvested, since the Asian gleaners collect more components of the nearshore resources than do the local people (J. Taman pers.

--- SENTENCE 2637 ---
For example, the Asian fishermen glean marine algae (see *Patterns of Utilization*), small fish and crabs, which the local gleaners do not (J. Gourley and J. Taman pers.

--- SENTENCE 2638 ---
This apparent change in the nature of the inshore fishery has had unknown effects on the coral reef resources.

--- SENTENCE 2639 ---
However, P. Dalzell (pers.

--- SENTENCE 2640 ---
comm.) suggested that the thorough gleaning of the reefs by the Asian fishermen may have a greater ecosystem effect than the less thorough gleaning practiced by the local Pacific Islanders.

--- SENTENCE 2641 ---
A similar situation may also arise on Tinian in the near future, due to the construction of a casino and the importation of large numbers of Asian workers to build and operate the hotel (V. Benavente and S. Burr pers.

--- SENTENCE 2642 ---
The responsibility for monitoring the recent coral reef fisheries (subsistence, recreational and commercial) in CNMI lies with the local Division of Fish and Wildlife (DFW: Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2643 ---
To do this, they have established several on-going surveys: the Commercial Purchase Survey, the Inshore Creel Survey and the Offshore Creel Survey (Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2644 ---
The Commercial Purchase Survey collects commercial fisheries data on pelagic species, several coral reef invertebrates (eg. octopus and lobster), and both shallow- and deep-water bottomfish, which are marketed on Saipan, Tinian and Rota (Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2645 ---
Each island has a separate data collection system, based on a dealer invoicing strategy or "trip ticket" system.

--- SENTENCE 2646 ---
Data on locally

caught fish are recorded by first-level purchases or dealers (i.e. retailers, wholesalers, or roadside operators) on specially designed invoices, which are collected by DFW on a regular basis.

--- SENTENCE 2647 ---
Catch data (date, dealer's name, fisher's name, species, total weight in pounds, price per pound, and value) are collected on all marine products, which enter the commercial market from each fishing trip.

--- SENTENCE 2648 ---
The survey was established on Saipan in 1983, and was expanded to include Rota and Tinian in March and August 1993 respectively (Hamm et al. 1996 in Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2649 ---
DFW estimate that over 90% of the all commercial landings in Saipan are included in the survey.

--- SENTENCE 2650 ---
However, data collection is logistically difficult on Rota and Tinian, and the number of vendors participating in the survey is low (five and fourteen respectively).

--- SENTENCE 2651 ---
To date, no landings estimates have been generated for Tinian and Rota, and the data from Saipan is primarily used to estimate total annual landings for pelagic and bottomfish species in CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 2652 ---
This type of survey has several problems, which should be considered when interpreting the data (Gourley 1997):

## 1.

--- SENTENCE 2653 ---
The data is collected by non-biologists, who are relied upon to identify species and accurately record the data.

--- SENTENCE 2654 ---
As a result, there are some problems with data quality.

--- SENTENCE 2655 ---
For example, certain groups of reef and bottomfish are often lumped into broad categories.

--- SENTENCE 2656 ---
Type of Data

The data reflects where the fish were sold and not necessarily where they were collected.

--- SENTENCE 2657 ---
For example, most of the fish caught on Tinian and destined for the commercial market are sometimes sold on Saipan, while some of the fish caught on Rota may be marketed on Guam.

--- SENTENCE 2658 ---
This is because of the higher demand (and better prices) for reef fish on Saipan and Guam, than on the other two smaller islands.

--- SENTENCE 2659 ---
In contrast, all of the fish sold on Rota were probably caught on that island.

--- SENTENCE 2660 ---
Despite these problems, the survey does provide a basis for estimating the total catch of reef fish in CNMI (DFW 1994a), and catch statistics for this fishery are summarized annually in DFW/WPacFIN reports (eg. DFW/WPacFIN 1992).

--- SENTENCE 2661 ---
With the exceptions of 1989 and 1990, DFW data show a fairly steady volume of recorded reef fish sales in Saipan from 1983 to 1993, varying between 100,000 and 140,000 pounds annually (DFW 1994c) 1989 saw a remarkable peak of 250,000 pounds, followed by 190,000 pounds in 1990 (DFW 1994c).

--- SENTENCE 2662 ---
The DFW started the *Inshore Creel Survey* on Saipan in 1984 (DFW 1994c, Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2663 ---
This program was based on a roving creel survey of the inshore fishery, including recreational, subsistence and commercial fishermen, along the shoreline of Saipan Lagoon (from Wing Beach to Agingan Point).

--- SENTENCE 2664 ---
The survey primarily focused on the non-motorized component of the fishery, and involved monitoring a variety of fishing gears, including hook and lines, cast nets, surround nets, spears (hand and powered), drag nets, and gill nets and gleaning.

--- SENTENCE 2665 ---
The survey also identified gleaning activities in the lagoon, such as the collection of algae and infaunal bivalves.

--- SENTENCE 2666 ---
The sampling design for the survey involved monitoring the area during daylight hours for four

days each month, including two workdays and two days on weekends or holidays (DFW 1996 in Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2667 ---
During the course of the survey, data were collected on the catch by species, number and weight in the inshore fishery (Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2668 ---
Fishing effort by gear type, man-hours and location were also monitored.

--- SENTENCE 2669 ---
While the information collected in this survey may be valuable for tracking the inshore fishery, the data have not yet been adequately analyzed and there are no accurate estimates of fishing effort or species composition (DFW 1994c, DFW 1996 in Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2670 ---
Unfortunately, this survey was suspended in 1995, apparently due to significant data quality problems (DFW pers.

--- SENTENCE 2671 ---
The Offshore Creel Survey was developed to compliment the Inshore Creel Survey by focusing primarily on the boat-based pelagic, shallow-water (≤100m) and deepwater (≥100m) bottomfish fisheries (Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2672 ---
The survey was limited to Saipan, and was based on four random sampling days each month (2 workdays and 2 weekend or holidays).

--- SENTENCE 2673 ---
Until 1995, data collection efforts were concentrated at boat ramps located on the leeward side of the island (Sugar Dock, Fishing Base, Smiling Cove and Tanapag Village).

--- SENTENCE 2674 ---
More recently, data collection has been limited to only two of these locations (Sugar Dock and Smiling Cove Marine (DFW pers.

--- SENTENCE 2675 ---
Unfortunately the results of this survey are considered to be of questionable quality for the following reasons:

## 1.

--- SENTENCE 2676 ---
Bias Towards Pelagic Species

--- SENTENCE 2677 ---
A recent review of the database by WPacFIN personnel determined that the data from the survey were considered "not reliable", because the survey methods were biased toward recording information on the troll fishery by the hours spent sampling each day (Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2678 ---
With virtually all of the effort directed toward the pelagic troll fishery, it appears that very little data was obtained from the bottomfish fishery (DFW 1996 in Gourley 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2679 ---
As a result of this bias, almost all of the data (99%) from the survey was composed of pelagic species.

--- SENTENCE 2680 ---
Data Collection Problems

Unfortunately, there were also some inconsistencies in the way in which the data were collected.

--- SENTENCE 2681 ---
For example, it appears that two length measures (standard and fork length) were used intermittently over the lifetime of the survey, without proper documentation of the dates when each method was used (DFW pers.

--- SENTENCE 2682 ---
As a result of these problems, analysis of the data is not appropriate and no accurate estimates of landings or effort for this fishery are available (Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2683 ---
The recent fisheries statistics for CNMI will now be summarized for each of the major taxa (reef fishes, corals and "live rock", invertebrates, and algae), based on the available data from these and other surveys:

## 3.2.1 Reef Fishes

Commercial, subsistence and recreational fisheries harvest reef fishes in CNMI, and the statistics for these fisheries are collected using different surveys (see above).

--- SENTENCE 2684 ---
The available fisheries statistics for each of these fisheries will discussed in turn.

--- SENTENCE 2685 ---
In addition, the shallow-water bottomfish fishery will also be described, since a component of the catch of this fishery could be considered reef fish (see *Executive Summary* and *Overlap with Existing FMPs*).

--- SENTENCE 2686 ---
A present, **commercial fisheries** for food fish range from individual free-diving spearfishermen operating from shore to multi-vessel operations (vessel size usually <30 ft) employing either local or alien laborers (Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2687 ---
The U.S. Department of Commerce (1995 in Gourley 1997) reported that the landings for reef fish species in CNMI in 1994 included "other snappers" (51 lb), squirrelfish (196 lb) and "other marine finfishes" (223,301).

--- SENTENCE 2688 ---
The "other marine finfishes" category may contain pelagic, reef fish and/or bottomfish species.

--- SENTENCE 2689 ---
Gourley (1997) noted that these landings do not agree with those based on DFW data (see below), and he recommended that USDOC figures should be checked for accuracy.

--- SENTENCE 2690 ---
CNMI's commercial reef fish fishery will be described based on the Commercial Purchase Survey, because of the problems associated with the other local surveys (see above).

--- SENTENCE 2691 ---
However, Gourley (1997) noted several problems when analyzing this data, including:

- 1.

--- SENTENCE 2692 ---
The majority of the "reef fish group" (89-91% in 1992 to 1994) could not be identified to either species or species group (see Table 54 below).
- 2.

--- SENTENCE 2693 ---
A group named "mixed (unknown)" could not be classified into either the reef fish group or the shallow-water bottomfish group.

--- SENTENCE 2694 ---
As such, 4% of the total reef associated commercial finfish landings in 1992 could not be classified.

--- SENTENCE 2695 ---
Similarly, 4% and 7% of the value of the catch for 1993 and 1994 could not be classified either.

--- SENTENCE 2696 ---
Despite the limitations of the Commercial Purchase Survey (see above also), the results of this survey can be used to describe trends in annual species landings over time and related to overall growth or decline of particular fisheries (Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2697 ---
Gourley (1997) reported that, assuming an annual constant sampling error, there did not appear to be a substantial increase in reef fish landings in CNMI from 1992 to 1993 (Table 54).

--- SENTENCE 2698 ---
However, there was an increase of 28% in total reef fish landings recorded between 1992/1993 and 1994 (Table 54).

--- SENTENCE 2699 ---
The reason for this increase is unknown.

--- SENTENCE 2700 ---
However, if the same basic fishing effort for 1994 is assumed for 1995, a minimum increase of 20% in reef fish landings could be expected in 1995, due to the JQC Fishing Company's seven month long operation in the northern islands (Gourley 1997, see below).

--- SENTENCE 2701 ---
This projected increase, bought about by one company, is almost the same magnitude as the increase in landings from 1992/1993 to 1994.

--- SENTENCE 2702 ---
Commercial landings of reef associated fishes in CNMI from 1992 to 1994 (from Gourley 1997 taken from Hamm et al. 1994, 1995, 1996).

A recent study by DFW (1994b) provides the best available information on the commercial spearfishery on Saipan and Tinian (DFW 1994b).

--- SENTENCE 2708 ---
This study obtained data on species composition, catch per unit effort (CPUE), and length and weight of the catch, over a nine-month period in 1993 (Gourley 1997).

--- SENTENCE 2709 ---
The study compared two components of the fishery: a day active freedive operation and a night active hookah operation (DFW 1994b).

--- SENTENCE 2710 ---
A total of 107 species were encountered in the study, and the relative abundance of families in the catch differed somewhat between night and day (DFW 1994b).

--- SENTENCE 2711 ---
During the day, the most abundant families were acanthurids (26% by weight), kyphosids (24%) and scarids (22%: Table 55), while acanthurids (43%) and scarids (20%) dominated the operation by night (DFW 1994b, Table 56).

DFW (1994b) found that nighttime CPUE (kgs per spear-hour) varied among sites in a manner that was consistent with the hypothesis that the less proximate and typically windward (and thus probably less-fished) sites would have higher fish densities.

--- SENTENCE 2727 ---
However after adjusting for the effects of other factors (eg. the number of fishes and lunar phase), the only significant difference among locations was the high CPUE recorded on the windward side of Saipan (South Saipan) relative to Tinian and the other locations on Saipan (DFW 1994b).

--- SENTENCE 2728 ---
In contrast, daytime CPUE did vary significantly between Saipan and Tinian, both before and after adjusting for other factors, suggesting higher fish densities in Tinian waters.

--- SENTENCE 2729 ---
However, this is a very tentative conclusion because of other confounding factors (DFW 1994b).

--- SENTENCE 2730 ---
Further evidence provided by DFW (1994b) suggests that some of the reefs of Saipan are more heavily fished than those on Tinian.

--- SENTENCE 2731 ---
For example, species composition was found to vary among sites, with some species being notably absent from areas that appear to be more heavily fished, such as Saipan Lagoon (DFW 1994b).

--- SENTENCE 2732 ---
Similarly, differences in the mean fish size were also found among several fishing areas for several species, with smaller individuals being recorded in areas that appear to be more heavily fished (Saipan Lagoon and the West Saipan Area: DFW 1994b).

--- SENTENCE 2733 ---
Significant temporal differences in CPUE were observed for the night operation only, with the highest catch rates recorded in June and July (DFW 1994b).

--- SENTENCE 2734 ---
However, DFW (1994b) suggested that this was not due to any significant temporal differences in fish density, since there were no significant temporal differences in CPUE observed for the day operation.

--- SENTENCE 2735 ---
Instead, they suggested that other factors, such as the motivation of the fishermen, may have caused the observed temporal variation.

--- SENTENCE 2736 ---
Temporal differences in size were only observed for one species (Siganus punctatus).

DFW (1997) also made some comparisons between the CPUE for night-caught reef fish in 1993 and 1995/1996 (Table 57).

--- SENTENCE 2737 ---
They noted that CPUE was similar in the same general fishing areas over time, and no noticeable declines in CPUE were observed (Table 57).
